In the US, fast-food and supermarket workers are on strike
One in four American teenagers will eventually be working at McDonald's

In recent days, there have been massive protests across the US against low wages in Walmart stores and fast-food restaurants like McDonald's, Burger King, Taco Bell, Wendy's and Kentucky Fried Chicken.
No one can predict whether the protests will continue to grow or whether they will soon run out of steam.
The protests are supported by trade unions and several left-wing non-profit organizations.
In addition to raising the modest wages of low-level workers at Walmart and fast-food restaurants, the organizers of the protests are seeking to create unions.
So far, this industry has been poorly organized by trade unions.
46 cents a year?
The protests began last week after Thanksgiving, known as Black Friday, when sales in the US were so good that they attracted millions of customers, sometimes leading to fistfights.
On that day, some 2.2 million Walmart workers worldwide walked off the job and joined with unions and left-wing activists to strike stores that serve low- and middle-income people.
Walmart sells everything from diapers to hunting rifles to car batteries to vacuum cleaners, eggs and milk.
The average price of the goods in Walmart stores is between 8 and 27% lower than in large supermarkets.
That is why many of the low-paid workers at Walmart shop only at their workplace.
The prices and the range of goods made Walmart one of the largest companies in the US.
Critics say that Walmart is able to sell its goods so cheaply because its employees are poorly paid.
The latter also complain about poor working conditions, for example the lack of forklifts or hand scanners.

The protesters at the "Black Friday" protests called for wage increases and expressed their anger at the fact that the contribution to the company-run health insurance had increased from $30 to $100 per month.
A typical Walmart worker, who earns $9.50 an hour, could not afford the increase, they said.
Researchers at the University of California at Berkeley show that if the company raises the average hourly wage to $12, it would cost Walmart $3.2 billion.
That is about 1.1% more than they are currently donating to wages.
If Walmart were to fully pass on the wage increases to customers, each purchase would cost an extra 46 cents.
For them, that would be an extra $12.39 per year, compared to today.
Proponents of Walmart are pleased that there were only protests in nine states and that they did not result in any losses for the company.
The Black Friday sale lasted in its store from 8 p.m. on Thursday to midnight the next day, and during that period Walmart sold about 5,000 items per second.
In total, Walmart's registers processed nearly 100 million transactions on Black Friday.

The company spokesman, Dan Fogelman, claimed in an interview on the left-leaning Huffington Post website that a total of "fewer than five" workers had walked off the job and that the protest was merely "another PR stunt" by the union that organized it.
"Free cash!"

The protests continued this week in New York, where their target was not Walmart stores (which are not wanted in this progressive city and therefore do not exist yet), but McDonald's and other low-cost restaurants.
McDonald's says that the company sells billions of portions, and yet it does not grant you sick days, and you are not paid for your honest work!
Jumaane Williams, a member of the New York City Council
Currently, the minimum wage is $7.25 per hour under federal and New York state law.
In fast-food restaurants, the minimum wage is gradually rising, but not too much, and on average, their low-wage workers in New York earn $8.90 an hour.
Less than they deserve no one in this expensive city.
I am amazed at how much you can do in New York with so little money.
There was a time when almost a quarter of all US teenagers worked in a McDonald's kitchen after school, but the teens were still living at home.
Few saw it as a major source of income or planned to stay there for long.
I am constantly meeting people in interviews with McDonald's employees who complain that they can't make ends meet on this wage and sometimes even have to support their children.
On the other hand, there is a comment in the Wall Street Journal's forum by someone who says it is irresponsible to have children if you do not know how to feed them.

The protesters, who began at 6.30 a.m. Thursday outside the McDonald's at 40th Street and Madison Avenue, were calling for fast-food workers to be paid a minimum wage of $15 an hour, which is more than a doubling of the current minimum wage.
They also called for the formation of trade unions in the fast-food industry.
The US law prohibits management from standing in the way of this goal and from firing or disciplining union members.
On the other hand, management makes it difficult for them.
However, the establishment of trade unions in the fast-food industry is also difficult for objective reasons.
The most important reason is the high turnover.
Discontent
There were also protests at many other fast-food restaurants in Manhattan on that day.

The climax of the protests was a lunchtime rally outside the McDonald's at Times Square, where some local Democrats spoke, including Council Member Jumaane Williams, who said, "McDonald's says it sells billions of portions, and yet it won't give you sick days, and it won't pay you for your honest work!"

The protesters were also supported by other prominent New York Democrats, including mayoral candidate Bill De Blasio, who said that "we should stand shoulder to shoulder with fast-food workers to ensure they get a fair wage and achieve the economic prosperity that every New Yorker deserves!".
According to the New York Times, it was the largest action of its kind in the history of the US fast-food industry.
Yet only a few hundred people were on the ground, of whom not all were employed in the fast-food industry, where tens of thousands work in New York.
It is not yet clear whether the spark of these protests will mobilise large numbers of people.
"The brain has been only partially fooled"
The popular topic of augmented reality among fans of modern technology is usually perceived through the lens of a special glasses.
First, Google presented a working model at its annual conference in the summer, and in November it was announced that Microsoft had also filed a patent for a similar model.

In conversation with the leader of the group for interactive 3D technologies at the Microsoft Cambridge Lab, Shahram Izadi, it becomes clear that the headset was only a stopover for the company’s scientists.
It is the opportunity to manipulate virtual objects in the air with your bare hands and create virtual spaces.
- Please briefly describe the research your group is conducting.
- We are dealing with the interaction between man and machine, but we want to extend the boundaries of that interaction.
So far, humanity has been stuck in the phase of working with pixels on flat screens that can sometimes be touched.
We, however, want to look 5-10 years ahead and anticipate the radical changes in this interaction.
For example, the Xbox console and Kinect are a step forward, and nowadays no Xbox is sold without Kinect, because everyone is interested in motion control.
- What is in store for us in the future?
- Although Kinect has brought interaction to a physical level, much of what happens is still on the flat screen, sometimes in 3D.
The input of information (the system receives more data) could be improved, the output is still not decisive.
We are trying to change that, working on true three-dimensional representation systems based on various technologies, including projections.
We must bring the computer world into our physical world and make it more tangible.
To do this, it is necessary not only to recognize the user, but also his environment.
Then we could easily supplement the real world with virtual objects.
And first of all we should get rid of these silly virtual reality helmets!
- What do you think about speech recognition?
It is popular, but is it over-rated?
- It is certainly not a panacea, because it raises issues of privacy, because you do not always want to inform everyone around you about your actions and intentions.
In fact, any kind of interaction with computers is good, but each in its own niche.
For example, we worked on a project in the area of controlling objects in public places, experimenting with short and brief gestures instead of expansive gestures.
The gestures were recorded not by the object camera, but by a wristband that recorded the movements of the bones and muscles.
It is still relatively large, but could be reduced to the size of a wristwatch.
But overall, the future will be a mixture of different types of control, for example gesture and speech.
- How is that possible?
- Would you please hand me this bottle of sparkling water?
They say it and at the same time they point to it.
- I usually just say it.
- Oh, that would be very difficult to see.
- Does this mean you want the user to adapt to what a machine can do at any given time and what it cannot do?
- Not necessarily, but it is about mutual rapprochement.
I think that we will have to focus in the coming period on developing new types of sensors that will allow us to detect reactions from people more accurately.
These can be laser sensors, as they offer good resolution in depth, which is very important.
- What are your expectations of modern cameras based on your work with the Xbox Kinect sensors?
Is there a lack of depth, or something else?
- The current generation is basically a good starting point for our work in the area of three-dimensional recognition.
Of course, 8 megapixels at 1000 fps would be great.
But the main thing is not the megapixels themselves, but the quality of the matrix and the depth.
In that sense, all the technologies we have today are not good enough for us, because the developers of the algorithms have more work to do.
It must not only take into account the resolution along the X and Y axes, but also along the Z axis.
The speed and the number of frames per second are also important.
Human movements are extremely dynamic and, frankly, the current 30 fps is not enough for gestures.

Stephen Betishes developed a touch sensor in our lab in Redmond with a programmable processing delay ranging from 1 to 100 milliseconds, with today's commercial sensors closer to the second value (60 to 100).
Not everyone understands how much this affects the interaction between man and machine.
For my work I needed exactly such a device, but without touch control and with more images per second.
- Should the number of cameras not be increased?
- Kinect currently uses three "cameras", with one being an infrared emitter and the other being a receiver for the reflected signal.
And the third camera is actually a regular RGB camera.
It is not used to calculate the object depth.
More cameras might solve the problem...
Or exacerbate the problem, because more calculations would be needed.
It would be nice to have a flexible system, like Kinect, where we could play with different camera angles to see how it helps us in the 3D estimation of a position.
- If I remember correctly, Microsoft did not present its glasses to the public, unlike Google.
Do not think that in terms of the application of the technology of augmented reality in everyday life the best prospects are for the glasses?

- Of course, it is not pleasant to have to hold a smartphone in the raised hand all the time, but I think the best variant would be a "changing" augmented reality, where we could switch from the glasses to the smartphone,

The glasses are a personal gadget and that is their strength (private can only see what you see), but at the same time their weakness, because augmented reality through glasses prevents you from working together with others on virtual objects.
- Let us imagine for a moment that the manipulation of virtual holograms in the air is not only accessible to Tony Stark from Iron Man, but also to ordinary people.
There is a problem that critics of this idea often point out: there is no palpable reaction!
The hands feel nothing at all!
What answers will your group give to this objection?
- In my lectures I often say that extended reality represents the seventh breakthrough in the interaction between man and machine.
I think the eighth breakthrough could be the integration of tactile perception.
An interesting method is currently the use of the second hand as an unusual projection surface.
It is very sensitive to pressure!

There are also technologies that are actually designed to give "images in the air" some substance, for example, the interference of some directed ultrasound beams at a certain point where the finger is located creates a sensation that is currently so weak that it feels like someone is blowing on the palms.
There are also wrist bands that stimulate the nerve endings in the fingers, which is another potential direction.
- Have you tried to outwit the brain?
To make it think that it is feeling what it should feel when it sees something?
- That is a good idea, we have not tried it before.

This is another task that we will have to work on for a long time, namely to make a person who is physically in a closed space believe that he is in an open, practically infinite space; here we are working on concepts with running tracks (other than in gyms), movable platforms and large balls.
So far, the brain has been only partially tamed, and many years of hard work lie ahead.
This is precisely what makes research in the field of virtual reality so attractive to a researcher: many of the topics are still at an early stage.
Taste instead of culture - rosbalt.ru
Rosbalt continues the project "Petersburg Avant-garde" dedicated to the city's avant-garde artists and cultural figures.
The list includes high-profile artists whose achievements transcend the city’s borders and who are often recognized in Europe, but are not known in the rest of Russia.
The new hero of Rosbalt is the extravagant artist Kirill Miller.
The whole city knows Kirill Miller, the bearded man in red, who can be found at the Russian Museum, at the Summer Garden, at scene events or at vernissages.
Wherever the pictures of Kirill Miller are exhibited, they attract large crowds.
Kirill Miller is one of the typical St. Petersburg social-philosophical artists who create new myths.
Kirill Miller is a bright personality of the St. Petersburg avant-garde at the end of the 80s and the beginning of the 90s.
He is also a man of the city and, by his presence on the street, he brings a smile to the faces of his fellow citizens and makes them happy.
Recently he grabbed a harmonium and became a St. Petersburg harmonium player, as he felt ready for this difficult role in terms of his artistic life, his philosophy and his image.
- Kirill, why are you always in red and not, for example, in yellow or turquoise in the city?
I chose the colour red as a fashion designer who deals with optics and image.
In this world, red is the compromise between artist, image consultant and society.
In society, anything that deviates from the norm is the cause of aggression and bad behavior.
But I want to engage with people through my provocations.
Each of my past provocations has been an invitation to dialogue.
- When did you know that you wanted to be an artist?
- At an exhibition at the Newskij Palace, where my works were exhibited.
I realised that I had to take this path.
Then the time of the old free, but not officially recognized painters was over, and new and free painters like me were incomprehensible.
I became friends with the painters of the new generation, with the representatives of the "Gazonewschina"; this led to "Puschkinskaja 10", and then it was all over.
I am drawn to the theatre, to fashion, to music, to everything except literature.
- And all this came together in your Art Clinic... - It was important for me to be at the center of the cultural life of St. Petersburg, where the best creative people should gather.
In 1995 I occupied a room in Pushkinskaya 10, and there was a musical-artistic club for the bohemians, the House of St. Petersburg Bohemians, until the renovation.
Many were born there: N.O.M., Tequilajazzz, and I also remember how Schnur came to the place with his project "Ucho Van Goga".
Schnur and his friends sang simple songs to the play-back, wore tight jerseys and among them was the today popular composer Igor Wdowin.
When the group started playing live, it became "Leningrad".
Trachtenberg moderated many programs before the time of "Halli-Galli".
We gave him Trachtenberg, and it began his great career, but he learned the basics with us.
The Galerie "D 137" or the Club "Griboedov" have their origins in the Art Clinic.
This is where our employees and regular guests went.
I am a hero of the last century, when culture still meant something.
In 2000 there was a survey in the press about the award "People of our city".
I won the category "Artist of the Year", and that was the peak.
It is not easy to work in new times according to old rules; I am a man of truth, honesty and culture of the last century.
In today's world it is easy to become famous, but fame and culture are not the same: one can be famous without making a cultural contribution.
- Your work has a distinctive style.
- Many of my pictures are real pearls and express clearly the actuality and sharpness of the thoughts.
I will have an exhibition on the subject of 'The Russian Museum as Clowns'.
Clowns are timeless.
I used to be social, but now it hurts and it makes me afraid to be.
In a clown it all dissolves and loses its tragic quality.
I love the grotesque, and I have grotesque ideas.
Let us, for example, save the world by making it compulsory for everyone to dress up.
Now everyone is concerned with clothes and looks, not with the inner person.
But perhaps one should not give a hand to a man, but should spit in his face.
The deception disappears by dressing up.
- Recently we saw you in the role of a city organ player. - A cultural city should have such a hero.
Who, if not me?
- Can commercial art be beautiful?
- Today commercial art must be careful, considerate and flattering.
We see the disintegration of cultures.
In the past, people formed large groups: the bohemians loved the one and the simple people loved the other.
Now there are micro-communities, and it is difficult to please everyone.
I am not a hundred dollar bill that everyone likes.
Now you have to decide who you will please.
Now every star has about 100 fans.
- The performances of Stas Michailov are attended by several thousand people!
- Women come to him, and the sexual sphere plays a role there.
For cultural reasons, 300 people come and not 10,000, so there is less management, less money, and everything goes to the ground.
I have supporters, and the most important thing is not to betray them and not to destroy what has been achieved.
In my youth I painted such pictures that were hung in a collector's collection alongside works by Falk and Larionov.
I started with images that normally come at the end of a career.
Today there are often misunderstandings.
It is called: intellectual culture and consumption culture.
Consumption has no culture, that is something completely different.
I am a man of the past culture and grew up with artists who lived in poverty and died in poverty and refused money to be able to paint.
This is the culture that I support.
- Kirill, what is missing from St. Petersburg?
- Good cultural experts.
It is said: servants of culture.
But not everyone can engage in culture.
In the real tsars it was different, because the tsars may not have understood much about culture, but they understood that real experts were needed.
There are good advisers in Moscow.
In St Petersburg we have people who could be experts, but they are blocked because we need more senior experts to assess them and open the way for them.
Now it is only a matter of taste.
The same is true of the Erarta, but with the difference that they are honest about not accepting all contemporary art and some painters have to look elsewhere.
- What is St Petersburg to you?
- St Petersburg is not the cultural capital; there is much more culture in Moscow and a better environment for it.
Art cannot grow on our stones.
We need a cultural soil, because for example we have more writers than readers, and that is not right.

Art must be modern again, as it was at the beginning of the last century.

Birth in space
Earth in danger.
Global warming or collision with killer asteroid.
Caravans of starships with Earthlings on board are searching for an alternative planet.
To save humanity, the important question is how we can reproduce in the weightlessness or on the substitute planet?
I think there are not many choices.
In fact there are only two real planets that we could hypothetically inhabit.
"Mars and Venus", says the scientific assistant of the Astronomical Sternberg Institute Vladimir Surdin.
While the conditions on Mars are relatively hospitable, the surface temperature of Venus is 500 degrees.
Life would only be possible at great heights or in orbit around Venus, in space.
The question of reproduction in space was first addressed by the researchers in relation to the flora.
Half a century earlier, experiments were carried out on plants.
The fourth generation of the space-grown peas were no different from the terrestrial varieties.
This was followed by the breeding of insects, in particular fruit flies (Drosophila), in orbit.
In 1979, quail eggs were sent into space to study how weightlessness affects the development of embryos.
It develops into a normal chick.
But then the problem begins.
"The problem is that the chick must find its feet; it must be able to stand and begin to move," explains the RAN Institute's laboratory director, Vladimir Sychev.
Without a solid ground the chicks ran around wildly.
Ten hours later, the newborn's instincts were completely dulled.
The chicks did not respond to light and sound.
Four days later they just died.
"We have twice let chicks hatch and then put the whole thing off because it is simply impossible to work with them," says Vladimir Sychev about the failed experiment with chicks in space.
The last animal-carrying space shuttle flew 16 years ago.
In spring 2013 the experiments will be continued.
However, the biosatellite "Bion" will only contain same-sex species.
There was an experiment with rats that had already been inseminated in space.
In principle nothing special was found.
"That was with the biosatellites, but again it was just one experiment, and research must continue," says Vladimir Sychev.
After landing, the space rats had babies.
The problem of reproduction in space has not yet been solved.
The task is difficult.
Animals that are ripped from their natural habitat simply cannot follow their instinct to reproduce.
Unlike animals, humans can do this in principle.
Homo sapiens is capable of abstract thinking and can create a similar emotional background.
For ethical reasons, such experiments are not carried out.
But women have been flying to space for 50 years.
The greatest risk was posed by Tereshkova.
The most valuable thing that humanity has is the female organism.
The seagull flew away, and no one on earth could answer the question: Can it survive a space flight?
Will she be able to have a child after this flight?
"Finally, no one answered this question," says space veteran Wachtang Watschnadse.
In June 1964, just a year after her space flight, the first female cosmonaut, Valentina Tereshkova, gave birth to a daughter.
The father of the child, Andrijan Nikolajew, was also a cosmonaut.
In 1988 the second woman in space, Svetlana Savitskaya, who had been in orbit twice and even worked outside the spacecraft, gave birth to a son.
However, there is still a risk.
We have only a few astronauts who have returned from long flights and had healthy children.
"The more you fly, the more dangerous it is even in orbit," concludes cosmonaut Valery Polyakov, a hero of the Soviet Union and a hero of the Russian Federation.
Yet humanity must seek new ways in biotechnology, radiation protection, and the creation of artificial gravity.
The Hydrolabor in the cosmonaut training center is an obligatory station during the preparation for the flight.
Here in a weightless state, the cosmonauts gain the routine for working in the open space.
Water represents the weightlessness.
Even though adults may find water pleasant, it is a foreign environment; but infants find water a natural element.
It is as if the little ichthyander were testifying that life on land arose from the ocean.
There is a connection between the fact that a child is in the womb for about 9 months in the amniotic fluid and the fact that it can then get used to water more easily.
In principle, it is logical, because from birth to the first swimming, only 2 weeks pass.
"It's not enough time to forget something," says Marina Aksenova, a baby swimming instructor.
While for a newborn the weightlessness is a much more natural state, the woman cannot do without gravity.
In the state of weightlessness the abdominal and pelvic muscles rapidly atrophy and thus the ability to push the baby out is reduced.
Well, let's get around that by using induction agents.
The birth could also take place in a special chamber to extract the child.
"But what happens then?", asks the not insignificant question of Valery Poljakov.
On the other hand, the child also needs artificial gravity.
Without feeling the earth's attraction, the organism cannot build the skeleton and muscles.
A newborn baby cannot be strapped into an exercise suit and taken to the space station for training.
He is simply missing what is essential to his life.

"This experiment, which we are doing together, namely the birth of a child in a foreign environment, will lead to the birth of a disabled person, a completely maladjusted person," says the head of the bioethics committee of the RAN Institute for Medical and Biological Problems, Igor Pestov, in advance.
Until now, the birth of children in space has been mere theory.
Eventually, it will become a reality when the inhabitants of the Earth leave their spacecraft to travel to a distant planet that will be their home for their offspring born in space.
NKÚ Chief: Control of the black market is failing due to the fault of the policy
The Czech Republic has good control bodies and adequate legislation in connection with public procurement, but it falls short in its application.
In an interview for Aktuálně.cz, Miloslav Kala, the deputy chairman of the Supreme Audit Office (NKÚ), says that
"A law is never perfect, but it must be applied correctly - and I believe that is not the case here," says Kala commenting on the current situation.
A similar result is apparently also reached by a joint inspection by Czech and German inspectors.
As a negative example, it cites the appointment of Prime Minister Petr Nečas to the so-called "Black System".
Recently, the Prime Minister said that the ODS would not bother the entrepreneurs with controls - is the system now banned or allowed?

"A law must be valid, and if something is prohibited by law, then it cannot be that the Prime Minister comes and prevents the supervisory authority, whose duty is to ensure that the law is complied with, from doing its job," says Kala.
At the meeting of the Committee on Budgetary Control of the Chamber, you spoke about a joint Czech-German project, in which the laws of both countries on public procurement were compared.
What was the substance of the debate?
This is a parallel examination which we started about two years ago.

In other words, it is a matter of the European legislature setting out how public contracts should be handled. This is what the national legislatures are building on. And finally, there is the practical application.

We have compared all of this with each other, and although the test is not yet complete, we have been able to identify some very interesting differences. In general, the laws in Germany are perhaps even more "strict and perfect", but the actual application is better in some parameters.
This confirms that it is not enough to constantly create new and more precise rules. We must also deal with the actual application of the law.
In what way can the project be of help to you? What is it that you can get out of this project?
Such a joint control could help us to stop constantly trying to perfect the laws and lower and balance thresholds when it is not clear that this is particularly positive.
Economic efficiency means buying something at a reasonable price (which is not always the lowest price) and excluding illegal enrichment or even criminal activity.
But lowering the threshold for orders does not guarantee that we will achieve this goal.

Perhaps it is even the case that we are only burdening the system in this way with excessive "paperwork", and those looking for loopholes in the system have it much easier to exploit the system than if the thresholds were higher.
They are talking about the problems of the practical implementation of the Czech public procurement law.
How does the control system work in Germany?
Is there a similar authority here to our NKÚ, or does the system work differently?

As far as the authorities are concerned, the German equivalent of the NKÚ is the Bundesrechnungshof, which is similar to our own and has a collegial structure, albeit with a slightly different composition. In principle, both bodies work in a similar way.

Competencies are also comparable to a certain extent, but Germany is a federal state, which means that there are these audit offices in the individual federal states - that is where the German system differs from ours.
The BRH is only allowed to control federal funds, which is what our federal funds are.
Public funds, which are managed by the districts and municipalities, are subject to the control of the state auditor-general.
As far as German legislation is concerned, is it simpler than ours?
In general, I would not like to compare without any specific reference. Nevertheless, Germany is often referred to as a model, but it is not possible to say that Germany is better in everything.
Is it perhaps because the examiners are better there?
That does not determine it, but as I said, I do not like such comparisons very much.
It should be noted that even those countries that we consider to be models are also facing problems.
Otherwise, they would have nothing to gain from cooperating with our authority, would they not?
As regards Czech legislation, what impact did the amendment of the Public Procurement Act have on your authorities, have you already felt any effects?
Given that this is a relatively new piece of legislation, it is not yet having an impact on our inspections.
As our controls are carried out retrospectively, there will be a certain delay.

We are currently experiencing the effects of the new control instrument "identification of risks of non-profitability" - we have examined and analysed almost 14,000 public contracts - this will of course have an impact, as the thresholds are changing, the conditions for certain types of contract have been modified, etc.
Do you see the adoption of this law as a positive step, or will it add to the burden of bureaucracy?
I think that this law is certainly a step in the right direction and I hope that it will be confirmed.
However, the problem can arise that the rules become "stricter" and cannot be complied with.

Already under the previous rules, the persons subject to a check are accountable to the body (for example, in the case of an operational programme of regional policy, the regional council) for any breach of the public procurement rules being considered a breach of budgetary discipline.
Is it then sensible to make the law even stricter?
I do not believe that it should be done in this way.
The system must exclude those who want to attack and abuse the system, and not punish those who have made a formal error that does not affect the actual decision-making.
Such a system merely puts bureaucracy under even greater pressure.
Where is the way out here?
Let us first of all say which path is not the right one.
The Prime Minister recently said that the ODS would not burden entrepreneurs with controls on the so-called 'black economy' - what exactly does that mean?
Is the black system now banned or allowed?

A law must be valid, and if something is prohibited by law, then it cannot be that the President of the Government comes and prevents the supervisory body, whose duty is to ensure that the law is complied with, from doing its job.
He can say, "We are changing the law and allowing the matter," but he cannot say that we are doing nothing.
The public procurement law contains rather strict rules on the formal execution of certain procedures - and this is also right for the protection of the public competition.
On the other hand, it is also tragic if the bidder with the best offer is excluded solely because of formal defects.
The law will never be perfect, but it must be applied properly - and that is what is missing in our case, I believe.

Simon Ornest: At our concerts we want to gather positive energy
What do you think about the fact that in less than a month the world is going to end?
This is one of those disaster reports that we humans love to read.
With our band The Tap Tap we are rather making fun of it and saying that we are the only band in the world that can gather enough positive energy to stop or prevent the end of the world.
In December you will also realize a unique project with three concerts against the end of the world.
Can you give us more information about the project?
It is a nationwide charity event that we have been planning for two years.
To do this, we want to use the marketing potential of the Mayan calendar, which is predicted to end on December 21 at 11:10 a.m.
The day before, on 20 December, there will be three concerts at the same time in Prague, Brno and Ostrava.
The end of the concerts is scheduled to coincide with the end of the Mayan calendar on the Pacific island of Kiribati, which is 12 hours ahead of us.
Who came up with this idea?
Originally I designed it myself, then we worked together with our graphic designer Honza Augusta to create the idea.
We want to collect enough positive energy to prevent the end of the world, but we also want to think together with the public about the state in which we will leave this world to our children.

On the occasion of the end of the Mayan calendar we have also created a unique collection of shoes, t-shirts, bags and key rings against the end of the world, which can be purchased via www.e-tap.cz and which will also help us.
The band The Tap Tap has also recorded the so-called hymn against the end of the world with the title "The end of the world falls out" together with other interpreters.
The song is already very popular on YouTube. Will it also be performed at the benefit concerts?
Of course, and I will say this last, provided that everything goes well and the world does not end...
The hymn is to be sung simultaneously by all the performers at all three concerts.
The songs will be broadcast live on Czech Television.
The text of the hymn is by Tomáš Hanák, who also plays the main character Jesus in the video clip, Xindl X also sings with him...
How did you come to work with both of them?
We also cooperate with other personalities of the Czech cultural scene, which is related to the fact that we organize many charity events and concerts...
We are trying to involve these people in our projects.
It has been shown that most people are interested in working with us, and enjoy it.
What is the purpose of the proceeds of the concerts against the end of the world?
For the establishment of the barrier-free educational centre Studeo, where we have been working together with the Tap Association for six years at the Jedlička Institute.
The students of the Jedlička Institute are regularly supervised by tutors who help them with different leisure activities.
As students themselves do not have the means to visit the lector, we would like to help them in this way.
In the framework of the completion of the Jedlička Institute, a separate building will be built, in which we will move with this project.
At each concert there are several groups and performers.
How did you select these?
We wanted to put together a programme that would appeal to all generations including children.
In Prague, for example, there will be concerts by Chinaski, Support Lesbiens, Illustratosphere with Dan Bárta, The Tap Tap, Marián Bango and Jiří Suchý.
All further information can be found on the Internet site www.kpks.cz.
Will similar "big events" be planned in the future?
In May we will perform at the Prague Spring Festival for the first time, and we are preparing an interesting programme with interesting guests.
Next year we would also like to perform in the Czech House in New York, and personally - if we are already in the USA - I would also like to combine this with performances in Washington and Chicago.
Your international plans are not small, you have already performed in Madrid, Brussels, London or Moscow.
The Tap Tap is however a group made up of people with disabilities.
How do you manage these trips logistically and organizationally?
It is not as bad as it seems at first glance.
Five of our members are wheelchair users, which means that their wheelchairs must be transported in the luggage compartment. We also have to carry a lot of musical instruments and other luggage...
Nevertheless, it has always worked well, ČSA and British Airways have always been very well prepared, so I sometimes wondered if I was a bit too prepared.
Even in Moscow, where we were recently, there were no problems.
Your travels abroad give you a comparison of how it is in the various countries with regard to accessibility, how they treat disabled people, etc.
How have you experienced these things so far?
After Madrid, Luxembourg, London and other cities where everything works better than here, we were just in Russia to witness that the East is still in its infancy.
In comparison, Moscow is not at all disabled-friendly. It is still unusual to see someone in a wheelchair in the city centre.
It is not even a given that a wheelchair user will be given priority in an elevator, for example.
Fortunately, there are also organisations there that are trying to highlight the problems of people with disabilities.
And in what way must we catch up with the more developed countries?
There are still many things we are lagging behind on...
However, it must be noted that improvement in the situation is also dependent on the efforts of the people concerned.
In London and Madrid it is absolutely normal for people with severe disabilities to move around the public space, to go to the museum, to use the toilets, etc.
It is not very common for a large group of disabled people to be actively involved in society, and we are a little ahead of the West in this regard, with the band The Tap Tap!
Respect in public and accessibility is one thing, but it is only when we have great athletes, artists, actors, politicians or lawyers from our ranks that things will really start to change.
So far, these have been isolated cases of particularly strong personalities.
The Tap Tap is very popular at the moment. But if we go back a few years: what motivated you in 1998 to form a band?
Then I started as a supervisor at the Jedlička Institute, where I met many young people who were interested in devoting themselves to something.
And as I am a musician myself and play the saxophone, I have founded a music club together with a colleague.
Well, and over time, as our moderator, Láďa Angelovič, says, it gets out of control (laughs).
The band was known in the last years, or am I wrong?
It is true that working with well-known singers has helped us; we have also started to actively promote ourselves.
We have realised that if you do something and it is not visible to the outside world, your own performance does not exist in a certain sense.
Thanks to EU funding we can also afford good lecturers, high-quality equipment and so on.
Was was your goal with The Tap Tap?
From the beginning I have felt the potential that things can be done differently.
In show business today, one often copies another.
This is in a way logical, because everything new is considered with caution and accepted only after a long time.
There are only a few truly unique things, and I dare say that Tap Tap is one of them.
The first impression that the viewer usually has is sympathy; that is only natural...
But this pity is completely superfluous because people with disabilities are not lonely and abandoned creatures that we should feel sorry for.
These are people who can live a full life and develop, provided they have the means to do so.
I always say that if people with disabilities achieve something, it is not only a progress for them, but also for the whole society.
Was was also helpful in achieving this success was that you are a strict boss, as many people say?
If you want to do something well, you must not compromise on many things and must also demand a certain discipline.
I think this is perfectly normal.

Some come to us with romantic notions, and when they find out that they have rehearsals twice a week, preparation periods and a lot of time spent on concert tours, the enthusiasm of many quickly fades.
That is how it works everywhere, in every band that wants to work seriously and achieve something.
Currently, The Tap Tap has twenty members.
How many of them were there from the beginning, i.e. since 1998?
Only one: Láďa Angelovič.
We are an open group. People come and go. That cannot be prevented.
Anyone who has the will and the desire to participate is always welcome.
Takes place on the day before the predicted end of the world, Thursday 20.12.2012 at 21:00
The venues are: Incheba-Arena/Prague, Fléda/Brno and Plynojem/Ostrava; 12 Czech bands and other musicians
All three venues will be linked together at the end by live-link and a joint interpretation of the song "Weltuntergang fällt aus" by the band The Tap Tap will be played.

The concert is intended to raise funds for the construction of a multifunctional, barrier-free educational centre to be built under the name STUDEO at the Jedlička Institute in Prague. The cost is estimated at CZK 25 million.
The entrance fee is CZK 400, children under 12 are free, tickets are available in advance at Bohemiaticket.
Poland and space.

Last week, Poland was admitted to the European Space Agency (ESA) as its twenty-first member state at a Council of Ministers meeting of the Member States of the European Space Agency. Poland is the second member state from the former Eastern bloc (after the Czech Republic, which joined ESA on 12 November 2008).
Poland began close cooperation with ESA in 1994 and has participated in several ESA projects in the years that followed.
Poland’s journey to space began much earlier.
Even before World War II, Polish space enthusiasts were interested in space, but they often ran into a lack of understanding.
I am referring here, for example, to the lecture by A. Šternfeld on 6 December 1933 at the Warsaw Observatory, where the author presented thoughts from his pioneering work "Entrance to Astronautics".
The ideas of the young engineer (born in 1905) however, did not catch the audience’s attention, and years later Šternfeld remembered that only Dr. Jan Gadomski had shown interest in his work.
In 1934, he won the REP-Hirsch Prize for "Entrance to the Space Age"
Dr. Jan Gadomski (1899 - 1966) later became an important advocate of astronomy and space exploration.
In Polish journals he published hundreds of articles and wrote several books on these scientific disciplines.
Gadomski's worldwide recognition for his contribution to the development of space was also acknowledged by the naming of one of the craters on the far side of the Moon after him.
In 1925, a rail-car was built in Poland, which was to be powered by a rocket engine.
The author of the draft and the details of this project have unfortunately remained unknown.
It is not even clear whether the rocket should be used to launch the train or to slow it down.
The information contained herein is taken solely from contemporary press.
In 1933, the Polish Infantry began to work on rocket-propelled projectiles.
The research was carried out by the Institute of Cell Technology in cooperation with Prof. Mieczyslaw Wolfke and Prof. Gustaw Mokrzyckiegi.
The documents that have survived show that research had advanced to the stage of practical tests.
Research was then interrupted by the invasion of the German Wehrmacht.

In 1937, the design of a photo-electric hunting rocket by Ing. Rohoziński appeared in the specialist press, and in the following year the work "Rakieta - torpeda powietrzna i rakietobomba lotnicza" by the author Leliwa-Krzywoblocka appeared.
Both projects were concerned with the military use of rocket propulsion.
Just before the war, all projects for military use of rocket technology were coordinated by the Temporary Scientific Advisory Committee (Tymczasowy Komitet Doradczo-Naukowy).
The committee was established in 1937, but its work was interrupted by the outbreak of war in 1939.
Other articles on space appeared in the Polish press thanks to the work of the Polish Space Society (Polskie Towarzystwo Astronautyczne) after the war.
The first mention of this society is in the November issue of the magazine Problemy, in which four extensive articles are devoted to space.
The article by Prof. M. Subotowicz contains the proposal to establish a space agency.
At that time, there were already the first projects on satellite technology, and it was clear that the exploration of space would have a future.
As early as its inception in 1956, the Polish Space Society (PTA) sought to join the International Astronautical Federation (IAF), and indeed, it was admitted as a full member in the autumn of 1956.
In the following year the first PTA President, Kazimierz Zarankiewicz (1902 - 1959), became Vice-President of the International Federation of Astronautics.
He held this post until his death in 1959.
Since 1956, the PTA has been actively involved in the development of the highly successful meteorological rocket (Rakieta Meteorologiczna), the first Polish rocket for scientific research.
The first type, the RM-1, was completed in 1957, the first launch took place on October 10, 1958.
The rocket with a maximum altitude of 1800 m was about 80 cm long and weighed not quite 5 kg.
Later a modified version, the RM-1A, was built, and in 1959 flight tests began in the Błędów desert with the two-stage rocket RM-2.
The rocket was 1.4 m long and weighed about 11.5 kg.
Another stage should be able to perform real scientific work - the RM-34 rocket should reach an altitude of up to 14.5 km and be used to observe high winds.
In 1962 however, the further development was stopped.
The Meteor-1 rocket, which was the successor to the first rockets of the RM type, was developed between 1962 and 1965.
The rocket was designed as a two-stage rocket, with a total length of 510 cm and a launch weight of 32.5 kg.
Three types of this rocket were developed (Meteor-1A, -1B and -1C), which differed in the size of the payload compartment for scientific instruments.
The Meteor-1A rocket had a transport volume of 0.4 liters, Meteor-1B had 0.34 liters and Meteor-1C had 0.62 liters.
The maximum altitude was 37 km for all three types.
In the years 1965 to 1968 the Meteor-2 rocket was developed at the Institute of Aeronautics, and its first flight tests began in October 1970.
Meteor-2 had a launch weight of 380 kg and was capable of carrying a payload of 10 kg to an altitude of approximately 60 km.
Meteor-2H and Meteor-3 were built.
It is also worth mentioning Poland's accession to the COSPAR (Committee for Space Research) in 1960, followed by the creation of a national COSPAR Committee two years later.
Poland also participated in space research with Soviet satellites, and in 1978 the Polish pilot Mirosław Hermaszewski became the second Interkosmonaut after the Czech Vladimír Remek.

Obviously, liberal democracies are currently falling into a situation, as Appian describes in his work on the crisis of the Roman Republic during the time of Caesar and Pompey: "The state had been in decline for a long time, and offices were being filled by force.
Against bribery, by illegal exploitation of advantages or with stone and sword.

"It was really beginning to be said that the only medicine for this serious situation was a dictatorship, and that a strong man should be elected"... Appian was thinking of Pompey, but the strong man was in fact Caesar, who permanently replaced the democracy with a dictatorship.
As we see, society today is based on the reckless preference of individual advantage, without regard for the interests of the whole society.

In November 1979, a mob of protesting Islamic students seized the US embassy in Tehran and took 52 diplomats hostage.
They demanded the release of the deposed Shah of Iran, who had fled to the United States after the revolution, who had been the patron of his regime for decades.
For the American government there was no way out of this situation - it could not afford to throw the Shah overboard, as that would have severely damaged its allies' confidence in other countries.
At the same time, it was unable to secure the release of the hostages in Iran, where the revolution led to the establishment of a theocratic regime.
It was a severe blow to the reputation of the United States, and the subsequent fiasco of the violent attempt to free the hostages made matters worse.
The diplomats were finally released after 444 days, following negotiations mediated by the Algerian government.
The fate of the hostages called forth a wave of solidarity at home and anti-Iranian sentiments.
The debacle in Iran contributed significantly to Jimmy Carter’s defeat in the 1980 presidential election.
The film Argo by director and actor Ben Affleck describes an episode of this story, which gave a small victory to the United States.
Immediately before the embassy was taken over, six embassy staff managed to escape.
It ended after many complications in the residence of the Canadian Ambassador.

The CIA, in cooperation with the Canadian authorities, managed to get the refugees out of Iran; they did so by using an elaborate story to conceal their true identities - they traveled with Canadian passports, posing as members of a film crew visiting the country for a science fiction film.
Combining genres
The plan, developed by the "exfiltration" expert Tony Mendez, also required Hollywood's cooperation.
To make the camouflage believable, articles about this film project appeared in specialist journals, press conferences were held, and the fictional production company had a real office.
The details of the operation have been kept secret for a long time. The film is based on the memories of Tony Mendez.
Afflecks Film is a special combination of several film genres.
On the one hand it is a realistic political thriller, on the other it is also a so-called "Caper Movie", i. e. the story of a successful horseplay like for example the film Ocean's Eleven.
The film alternates between documentary scenes from Tehran (in the title sequence iconic contemporary photographs are shown, and in the film version of the same scenes there are no major differences)
On the other hand, the light-hearted Hollywood passages that are ironic and slightly exaggerated.
And then there are the scenes from the CIA headquarters and other institutions - men in suits at the conference table, in the corridors, on the phone...
Ben Affleck has made a remarkable comeback with this film.
From a ridiculed actor he has become a respected director, and as an actor he is no longer the target of ironic comments.
Argo is his third feature film after the crime drama Gone Baby Gone (2007) and the thriller City of God (2010).
At the same time, it is Affleck’s first film not to be set in his hometown of Boston.
The sense of place was one of the qualities that distinguished his previous films from the standard Hollywood fare.
Affleck, however, also demonstrates this sensitivity in Argo, where Tehran is "played" by Canada.

The best scenes of the film take place in the streets and show the reconstruction of events that really happened - the opening sequence of the storming of the embassy is very impressive in its clarity, and yet conveys the sense of bewilderment and unpredictability that comes when history moves somewhere.
Affleck’s team also achieves a similar effect with the fictional scenes (the fake film crew at a bazaar in Tehran).
Too much action at too many places
The director also had to deal with the fact that the story does not offer many exciting scenes in the filmic sense.

With the few he works quite successfully, sometimes helping reality - which then does not always look as elegant (the scenes in which the impending crisis at the airport in Tehran is averted by a phone call in America, or even the chase on the runway, look a bit contrived).
The weakness of Argo is its too wide dispersion, necessitated by the need to show too much action in too many places.
While Alan Arkin and John Goodman are very charming in their roles as Hollywood insiders, their characters are given far too little room to breathe, and they are not alone in that regard.
Afflecks film loses some of its punch. It is a film that you can watch with some interest and enjoy the design and the retro style reminiscent of a thriller from the 1970s.
But enthusiasm is hard to arouse.

Guidelines for inflating balloons, bananas and for the circus

The server www.bankovnipoplatky.com, which every year announces a contest of the most absurd bank charges, has decided this year to organize a contest "Most absurd regulation or idea from the EU workshop".

"The idea came from the plan recently proposed by the EU to introduce a 40% quota for women in the management of large European companies," said Patrik Nacher, who is in charge of organising the survey, to the newspaper Právo.
One of the nominated absurdities is the European Court of Justice's judgment on the harmonisation of insurance premiums for men and women.
Until then, women enjoyed an advantage in life insurance because they were objectively less risky to the insurance companies.
"More amazing EU-workshop ideas can be nominated until the end of this year.
The actual vote will take place by the end of February 2013", Nacher said.

Among the controversial EU regulations is the mandatory blending of bioethanol in fuels, which is harmful to nature, the ban on reliable mercury thermometers, because they contain a relatively small amount of this hazardous substance, or the directive on the size of chicken cages, because of which eggs have become much more expensive this year.
In the past, criticism has also been directed at the fact that the term "butter spread" has been banned or that conventional light bulbs have been banned from sale.
Bananas must be 14 cm long

The EU bureaucracy often decides under pressure from one or other lobby from trade and industry, whose demands are usually represented in Brussels by one or more Member States (for example, the Czech Republic is currently trying to impose its will on Czech banks, even with a veto threat).
Lobby interests were also behind the requirement that bananas of the highest quality must be at least 14 cm long and not have a "curvature anomaly".
The European Commission defended itself by saying that it was only harmonising the non-uniform national rules which would hinder trade.
The standards for fruit and vegetables have already been relaxed by the EU, despite the opposition of some countries, on the grounds that the current directives would lead to food waste.

A candidate for victory in this poll is perhaps the EU regulation of last year, which must be accompanied by balloons sold with the notice that children under the age of eight must not inflate the balloon without adult supervision.
The EU referred to an American study, which concluded that balloons are the leading cause of suffocation in children.
A similar restriction already applies to children under 14 when using fairground rides.
There are also some quirky ideas at home

It is also rather absurd to have a directive that affects the European officials themselves - anyone who is in an official position in the EU cannot use the name Macedonia because of the sensitivity of the issue for Greece and must instead say FYROM (Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia).

The Bankovnípoplatky.com server nominated in cooperation with the Union of Liberal Economists Laissez Faire in addition to the above absurdities the EU regulation on the scope of food reserves in the territory of a Member State.
The EU set the maximum volume of food reserves that could be located in the Czech Republic on the day of our EU accession.
For example, the Czech Republic exceeded the volume of mushroom preserves that was permitted, which would have resulted in a heavy fine.
The organisers of the survey were also impressed by the idea that certain countries should be given money for not having a sea, or by the idea of giving funding for applications for funding.
These ideas, however, did not come from Brussels, but from Prague.
"We are disadvantaged because we do not have a sea.
We will ask for EU compensation, said the then Minister of Agriculture Jaroslav Palas (ČSSD) in the autumn of 2004.
He argued that the harvest of cereals had been very high and that the state stocks had been overstocked as a result of the so-called intervention purchases.
As the Czech Republic has another way to the sea, the EU should pay us hundreds of millions of euros.
The European Commission finally came to an agreement with the Czech Republic to organise a tender for the purchase of cereals from countries that do not have access to the sea.
The Ministry of Regional Development, led by Pavel Němec (US-DEU), offered the municipalities funding for the submission of applications to Brussels.
EU: Bizarre regulations are the exception

Although regulations are often the target of criticism in the Member States, the EU's efforts to regulate and thus also to make the whole of the European Union more effective and to develop are, according to some experts, rather deserving of recognition.

A more serious problem, according to these experts, is the EU funding for projects that have nothing to do with deepening European integration, but which have been forced through the budget negotiations of individual Member States.

The emotions aroused here are also due to the fact that, like other Member States in Brussels, the Czech Republic has to fight for the right to use specific names for traditional products and does not always win this fight.

Although the Czech Republic was able to defend the name "Olomoucké tvarůžky" after a six-year battle with Germany and Austria, our producers had to rename the "Inländerrum" (Tuzemský rum), whose tradition in our country goes back to the 19th century, to "Tuzemák".
The term rum may only be used for products made from sugar cane, not for products made from sugar beets.

In the official list of products registered in the EU, the society of world-famous cheese varieties feta and gorgonzola, the Lübeck marzipan or the Parma ham now also appear the Karlsbader zwickel, carp from Pohořelice and Třeboň, or even the Saazer hops.
With a EU brand, the Pardubice gingerbread or the Hořice rolls can boast.
"People want me to save the republic, but I'm just an amateur," Okamura says.
Senator, how is it that you have decided to stand for the presidency?
I do not want to be a Senator or a President.
If everything were working well in our country, I would not stand for election anywhere.
But I can no longer watch the Republic being plundered for 20 years, thieves roaming around while people's taxes and retirement age are increased.
I had no ambition to be a politician.
If I see something that I do not like, I try to propose a solution to change it.
And since I am over 40, and independent and non-partisan, I have no other way to influence things than to run for the office of Senator or President.
In the Senate you have managed to get there and then you have started your journey to the castle.
Are you not turning your back on your voters?
I have told myself all the time that I will take up the fight for the castle after the Senate elections.
Later I clarified that I would be a candidate for the position of President if I am elected Senator.
My goal is not the function. The function is a tool to realize my vision.
I need as much influence and as strong a mandate as possible.
The difficulty is not only that we as a people in the pub and in front of the television criticise but also that we belittle anyone who wants to change things.
There are also the media, which want to take away our honour, and which confuse the freedom of speech with the freedom to lie.
For example, I have been accused of bribing journalists or of being an adviser to Jiří Paroubek.
Let us talk about your vision.
You have taken up the fight for the castle with the thesis of material and criminal liability of politicians and with retroactive declarations of assets of 20 million crowns.
To do that, you have to change laws.
As President, you have no competence in this respect, and only the Senate as a whole can submit proposals for legislation.
How do you intend to resolve this problem?
As a simple citizen I have fought to ensure that the guide is a free profession, and this has been achieved.
The problem is petty politics - if someone on the right or left comes up with a good idea, it is deliberately rejected, and that just leaves the population waiting.
As an independent, I have a much greater potential to win support from all the parties represented in Parliament.
My advantage is that I can take from each party what is best for our country, without prejudice or party dogma.
Do you see yourself as a person more to the right or to the left in politics?
From a Czech point of view, I think that people see me more to the left.
For me, however, this left-right thinking is completely irrelevant.
It is important for me that we are moving forward.
I do not want to know whether someone is on the left or the right; I want to connect people.
I will always support publicly any good idea, whether it comes from the KSM or the ODS, and I will oppose any bad idea.
You are offended by the term 'populist'
But are you not confirming what you just said?
When you are writing a business plan for a company, you have an ideal goal and a vision.
And you want to get closer to this.
It may be called populism, but all the proposals I have mentioned are already working in the world, or they have been discussed by important experts.
But without support in Parliament you will only have slogans.
And that is not a way to go in politics in the long term.
Or do you think that you will be able to achieve, by talking to people long enough, for example, to make them accept the material and criminal liability?
I have no other choice.
Politicians, journalists and the public to convince and try to bring them on our side to achieve these goals.

As President, it would be no problem for me to call on the leaders of the political groups to make it a legal requirement for politicians, officials, judges and prosecutors to be held liable for their actions.
And those who are concerned should then have to say why they are opposed to it.
A strong personality who points out abuses can exert pressure on the political scene.
Take, for example, the direct election of the President, which was a result of public pressure.
I am quite clear that I am an amateur; I am neither a genius nor an intellectual.
I am trying to find allies for my views and vision.
I have just started with politics and I am trying to find support for my programme from the majority.
I have always tried to judge things myself; and if it does not work out, I will go back into the private sector in six years.
It sounds a bit like Okamura is trying to save the Czech Republic.
I am not a saviour.
I know that I cannot achieve anything on my own; therefore I have spoken to several well-known people to ask if they would like to stand for the Senate.
I have spoken to Radim Jančura, who however declined because of overwork.
I also supported the investigative journalist Jana Lorencová, who exposed the fraud in the trade of light heating oil.
My candidacy began with the assumption that people are deeply dissatisfied, but now I am not so sure.
Sixty percent of eligible voters did not vote, and the ones who did vote were mostly representatives of the establishment.
In the Senate we are only two independents.
The people have chosen a Senate composition that will make changes very difficult to implement.
I will, however, continue to fight for my vision, for example, for the direct election of mayors and district leaders.
Are you thinking about starting your own party?
I have not thought about this yet because I do not have time to check the past of every potential party member, and I do not have the money to do so.
I have not even got any money for the presidential campaign; on my transparent account there are only CZK 20,000.
You don't have any money?
You are talking about declarations of wealth, how would your declaration look like?
My personal assets are estimated at around CZK 60 million.

In Prague I have a property worth 25 million, an apartment worth about 10 million, another worth 8 million, a collection of art worth about 10 million, and an Aston Martin worth 3.5 million and a Škoda Superb worth about a million. And then I have a few million in the bank.
The Aston Martin was a childhood dream - I have always loved James Bond, driving the car, being suave with women and fighting evil at the same time.
You drive an Aston Martin, have a fortune of $60 million and have no money for your campaign?
You say you want to change the Republic, but you do not want to invest your own money in it.
That is not exactly convincing.
I have no €15 million for the campaign.
Should I be in debt?
I have already invested €2.5 million in the campaign.
The fact that I have no sponsors shows that my program is probably not very interesting.
I am not obliged to fund the campaign from my own resources.
The cost of the campaign is basically covered by my salary as Senator.
But I could not live on the Senator's salary alone; for example, I could not pay for my son's English school, which costs £30,000 a month.
If I wanted to earn money, I would not stand for anything.
So, you continue to be an entrepreneur to make a living?
Did you not say that you will be reducing these activities?
But that has nothing to do with the level of pay.
As promised, I have reduced my activities.
For example, my deputy will become the manager of the travel agency in the spring.
People want to see me as a Samaritan who is saving the Republic.
But I must also earn a living.
What monthly income were you used to as an entrepreneur?
About 200,000 to 400,000, and that is still the case.
As President, however, I would close my businesses.
