The MVRDV architects prove that real adventures are not only in the mind - in the case of Spijkenisse and the recently built Book Mountain - 2 photos
"I find the building funny, it looks futuristic, and finally there is something interesting to see again", says Lisette Verhaig, a passer-by.
Stefan Spermon, IT-technician at a nearby large company, says: "Yes, it is beautiful, the house."
But I wonder what we need a library for today.
Everyone has Internet, iPad and e-books.
No one goes voluntarily to one of these old-fashioned libraries, do they?
Spijkenisse, a sleepy town on the outskirts of Rotterdam, is an odd record holder.
The 80,000-inhabitant municipality has the lowest level of education in the Netherlands.

In order to counter this stupid situation, a few years ago, it was decided to contribute to general education and to reproduce the seven bridges depicted on the euro notes as pretty little miniature bridges made of painted reinforced concrete.
The success of the education offensive was limited.
And so the city fathers realized that there was only one way to control the statistics: a library must be built!

Winy Maas of Rotterdam’s MVRDV, master of the daring beam diagrams and producer of witty, often cynical buildings, took the matter with his usual calm and appeared at the hearing in 2003 with five books under his arm and a grin on his face.

And while the jury was still looking around in bewilderment and shrugging its shoulders, the cheeky Maas stacked his exquisite gifts in a pyramid and ended his actionist speech with the words: "Dear city council!"
This is, therefore, my proposal for the Spijkenisse book mountain, the so-called Boekenberg!
Nine years later the 30 million euro mountain has been built up.
It is part of a revitalisation project, which also includes a car park, a supermarket, a post office and a few adjacent houses and townhouses with a total of 50 apartments.
In early November, the Book Mountain was awarded the second prize "Best Library of NL 2012".
Furthermore, the project is nominated for the Dutch National Wood Award 2012.

This is the face-less town centre, which has hitherto offered nothing more than a postmodern pedestrian zone and a face-less town hall, behind whose white facades one might imagine a dairy factory, to be enriched by a piece of contemporary architecture.
Above all, Spijkenisse now has the first public cultural building in its history.
The long road to the book
First impression: book paradise under a cheese dome.
There is a lift that runs through the mountain, but the real pleasure of the space and reading is to climb the topography on foot.
The all-glass interior is bright and open, the brick floor and elegant street lamps speak the language of a public square.
The urban ambience is perfect.
People are already looking for a park bench, a dog and some boys and girls playing football.
And everywhere books, books, books.
"Normally the bookcases are along the facade, and in the middle there is a large, dark room, which is usually uncomfortable and impersonal," says Winy Maas.
We have turned the classic layout on its head and placed the reading area on the outside.
The inside of the library is cleverly used: in the middle there are offices, an internet library, a chess club, an environmental centre and a technical centre.
A particular pleasure are the black bookcases, which are sometimes wall cladding, sometimes balustrades, sometimes stair railings.
Optics, haptics and smell are foreign.
Even the most ardent architects and engineers shake their heads in bewilderment at the unknown substance.
"We wanted to work with recycled materials here," explains Joop Trouborst, project manager for the municipality of Spijkenisse, in response to a Standard inquiry.
And so we came across a suitable by-product from the agricultural sector one day.
For many years, in greenhouses and in fields in the Netherlands, a millimeter-thin plastic fleece has been used as a root cover.
This is cheap and time-efficient.
The thin fabric will last one or two seasons, after which it is ready for the rubbish.
For the library, the nonwoven was pressed into four-centimeter thick slabs - for the first time in these quantities.
Under the influence of heat and pressure the so-called Landbouwplastic (KLP) turns into a dark, homogeneous, load-bearing material that smells a bit like a new car and a bit like a sports shoe.
After 105 steps you reach the summit.
At the end of the almost 500-meter long walk you will be rewarded with a fantastic view of the city, as well as with Dutch croquettes and potted ficus trees.
They create atmosphere, but above all they provide the right humidity in the literary mountains.
Donations for the new soul
"It is not easy to believe, but this building is a showcase project in terms of ecology despite the many glass surfaces," says Trouborst.
Heating and cooling is done with geothermal energy.
Although the book mountain is under a glass roof, the sun seems to shine only briefly inside even on sunny days.
The wide timber beams that run across the glass façade provide shading and capture much of the sunlight.
The climate is very pleasant.
The rest is taken care of by fully automatic blinds.
Stefan Spermon, the initial skeptic from the IT industry, has already ventured into the new library.
Lisette Verhaig was also there.
And also the TCM teacher Cynthia Bogarde, who describes the Boekenberg as a "long overdue soul" of Spijkenisse.
The reason: To open a few weeks ago, everyone was invited to donate a book from their personal collection.
This will initially fill the optical gaps in the library, which currently contains 70,000 items.
The concept has worked.
The shelves are filled to the brim.
"Nothing is worse than a half-empty library," says architect Winy Maas.
"I think that thanks to our invitation, everyone now has a certain relationship with this new house.
Everyone knows that his book is part of this building.
And if it is only for show.
This is the discipline that MVRDV has mastered, which is called identity-building in the jargon of the profession.
Spijkenisse has written literary history.
As young and uneducated as she may be.
This is finally a point of identity.
Szabo: "Germans must play a greater role"
Germany abstained in the vote on the inclusion of Palestine.
According to Stephen Szabo, an expert on US-European relations, Berlin is walking a tightrope of diplomacy.
Deutsche Welle: At the beginning of the week, Germany had indicated that it would vote against the request for observer status for the Palestinians at the United Nations.
But Berlin was silent.
Why?
Stephen Szabo: Germany does not support what the Israelis have done in Gaza.
However, Germany must be careful because of its special relationship with Israel.
But at the same time I believe that it is not the American position either.
Germany wanted to demonstrate its independence - without being too critical of Israel.
During the Libyan uprising in March 2011, Germany also abstained on the issue of establishing a no-fly zone.
This was finally enforced by NATO.
Is it difficult for Germany to take a clear position on important international issues?
Yes, that is true.
This is because it is changing its foreign policy away from a policy that was essentially managed by the US to a German foreign policy.
The fact is that Europeans do not have a coherent and unified policy.
The Germans are thus finding themselves on the wrong side of the fence.
They are expected to play a more independent role, but they are not used to that.
I believe that they are still finding their feet in their role, but they are on the way to a more 'normal' foreign policy.
A foreign policy, as France or Great Britain have.
What does a "normal" foreign policy mean in concrete terms from Germany's point of view?
It shows the willingness to take positions on national interests that are independent of those of the US or European partners.
I believe that German foreign policy is motivated by economic policy, by exports and by its relations with certain regions, such as Russia, China or the Middle East.
Germany’s economic interests are to a certain extent different from those of the other major powers and therefore Germany must protect its interests.
Have these economic interests influenced the stance on the Middle East conflict and the vote in the UN?
On the one hand, Germany has large markets in the Middle East, particularly in the Gulf States.
Therefore, it must be careful not to offend the public, but also the elites, in the Arab countries.
It is certainly a factor.
But I would not want to give it too much weight, it is not a completely one-sided relationship.
But it is certainly playing an important role in German thinking.
Has Germany damaged its relations with the US by abstaining on important decisions, such as on Palestine?
I believe that there is a great deal of understanding in Europe and even in the United States of the German position.
I therefore do not believe that this was such a dramatic break as in the Libyan case.
Perhaps Germany will even gain some respect for itself.
For it signals that it is taken seriously as an international player and that its interests must be taken into account.
There are different opinions in Europe about the Palestinian initiative.
The US, on the other hand, has been clear in its support for a veto.
Are there disagreements between the US and many European nations?
These differences have always existed in American domestic politics.
I believe that the Obama administration is secretly quite sympathetic to the European position.
But given the political situation here, the Government cannot publicly take this position.
I believe that the real differences are not as great as they seem to be.
If you look at the relationship between Obama and Prime Minister Netanyahu, Obama is not exactly thrilled with Netanyahu’s policies.
Is it difficult for Germany to reconcile its close relations with Israel and the US on the one hand, and its position as one of the EU's most important partners on the other?
I think that is precisely what makes it so difficult for Germans.
It would be a little easier for the Germans if there were a coherent and unified European policy, which is not the case at the moment.
So they cannot be part of a wider line and must instead drive things forward from their own position.
That is what they are doing with the euro.
I believe that in the future Germany will take a leading role in pushing Europe to a European position.
This is not easy for Germany, given its relationship with Israel.
This has always been a sensitive issue.
But I think that Germans are aware that they must play a more independent role.
Does Germany see itself as an important international player - does it want to take on a major role?
Or is Germany still struggling to take on the leadership role?
Germany is not used to this, it is still uncomfortable and, for obvious reasons, it is still difficult for the country to play a greater role.
For example, when we look at the euro crisis, whenever Germany takes on a greater role, there are always different anti-German feelings.
This makes it difficult for the Germans.
This is the old problem: you do not want to be surrounded by hostile countries.
In that sense, Germany is in a much more difficult position than the United States.
It must be open to different neighbours and opinions and that is not easy.
Now the influence of the US in European politics is steadily declining, but the EU is not filling that vacuum at the moment, who else is?
The Germans will have to play a greater role.
Even if they don't like it, it makes them even less popular - c'est la vie!

Stephen Szabo is the Deputy Director of the Transatlantic Academy in Washington, a think tank where scholars and policy experts from Europe and North America work together to address the challenges of the transatlantic community.
Szabo is also a member of the German Marshall Fund, where he specializes in German politics, US foreign policy and transatlantic relations.
"Trademark protection" in China: If Puma and Armani suddenly become Chinese
Armani is a world-renowned brand, Polo Ralph Lauren too.
What is Armani Polo?
This is a name that is registered in China, but it has nothing to do with the original companies.
However, it is protected as long as the original owners do not complain.
And even then it is not clear whether they will be right.

"It is becoming increasingly difficult for foreigners to protect their brands in China," says Thomas Pattloch, a lawyer at Taylor Wessing who specializes in infringement of intellectual property rights in the Far East.
Every week a new case lands on my desk.
Imitators need only add a few extra letters to their names to be able to register their trademarks.
Thus, Gucci becomes Lu-Gucci, instead of Prada, Prada-Kny is entered.
German companies are also copied in this way, for example the sports goods manufacturer Puma.
Pattloch opens a folder with entries from the Trademark Office in Beijing.
On September 14, 2010, a Chinese company registered the trademark Zegna DF Puma, a trade name that was also used by Ermenegildo Zegna.
It is well known that the Chinese are world champions at copying and at infringing intellectual property rights.
In the big cities there are multi-storey shopping centres, which sell almost exclusively fakes.
But patent trolls are different: they sue to prevent Chinese companies from using a name that is already protected elsewhere.
The Chinese call it "Bang Mingpai", a brand of co-driver.
The word is derived from "Bang Dakuan".
These are women who fish for rich men.
The Chinese authorities are not aware of any wrongdoing
"This is damaging to business, we must fight it," says Pattloch.
"The brand is diluted, the exclusivity is lost, the damage to the image is enormous."
The financial losses and the process costs for the affected sectors are in the millions, especially for expensive flagship products.
According to the market research company CLSA, China is the third largest market for luxury goods, with a volume of €15 billion per year, and the fastest growing.
But the deletion of dubious entries in the trademark register is difficult and expensive.
The process can take up to nine years, with an uncertain outcome.
Pattloch reports cases where the court has rejected claims because the long period of use of the name has made it a "market reality".
If the plaintiff is unlucky, he may have to pay the plagiarist money because he infringed the latter's trademark in China, says Pattloch.
Sometimes the jungle law is in force.
Famous cases also involve graphic elements.
In 2009 Daimler lost a legal battle with construction equipment manufacturer Sany, the company that recently acquired German concrete pump manufacturer Putzmeister.
The Chinese are therefore still allowed to use an emblem that is similar to the Mercedes star.
The Volvo buyer Geely originally used a blue-and-white logo that was reminiscent of BMW; the dispute was settled, Geely had to change it.
The fashion brand Lacoste lost in China to imitators from Hong Kong and Singapore who turned the crocodile around.
The Chinese authorities are not aware of any wrongdoing.
The China Trademark Office (CTMO) in Beijing admits that it has been experiencing bottlenecks due to insufficient staff and space since 2010.
However, last year, we were able to return to normality from the emergency situation in the workplace.
The number of pending un-amended appeals has fallen by 22 per cent.
More than 57,000 such cases have been closed, 75% more than in the previous year.
However, there are still 81,500 appeals pending in the office.
To address this problem will cost a lot
As is often the case in China, the numbers are impressive.
Last year, the CTMO received more than 1.4 million applications for trademark protection, a 30% increase over 2010.
That is a record and means that China has topped the list of new applications around the world for the tenth year in a row, the agency said.
This also applies to the status of all valid trademarks, a total of 5.5 million pieces.
In 2011, 1.8 billion yuan in fees were collected.
In other words, each registration costs an average of 1,280 yuan or €160.
To address this problem will cost much more than the case of the German family-owned company Freudenberg shows.
For more than seven years, the group has been fighting a Chinese plagiarist.
While the Germans were able to achieve the seizure of illegal factories producing imitation car parts,
But the imitator continued to secure the Chinese rights to the Freudenberg brand.
The problem is that in Germany, family names cannot be protected, says Hanno Wentzler, the managing director of Freudenberg Chemical Specialities in Munich.

Facts about sexually transmitted infections
What are the most important sexually transmitted diseases?
Bacterial STIs include syphilis, chlamydia, and gonorrhea.
Common viral STIs include HIV, human papillomavirus, herpes, and hepatitis.
Filth mites and scabies are among the parasitic STI.
Who are the main groups affected?
Syphilis and gonorrhea are mainly transmitted by men having sex with men.
The Robert Koch Institute assumes that at least four out of five of all syphilis cases reported in Germany are transmitted by sexual contact between men.
Among heterosexual adults, chlamydia, trichomoniasis, candidiasis (fungus), syphilis and human papillomavirus are common sexually transmitted diseases.
The spread of HIV among heterosexual adults here is relatively low - but around 20% of new infections are among this group.
Chlamydia infections are much more common among young people than among other age groups.
According to European surveys, three-quarters of infections are among young people aged 15-25.
In addition, human papillomavirus is common among young people in this country.
How has the number of infections developed?
Not all sexually transmitted diseases are notifiable.
According to the Robert Koch Institute, the number of syphilis infections has increased from 1697 cases in 2001 to 3698 cases in 2011.
The number of new HIV infections has been declining since 2007.
In 2011 there were around 2700 cases.
That is about a tenth less than in the previous year.
What symptoms indicate a sexually transmitted disease?
The infections can cause genital ulcers, urinary discomfort, discharge, lower abdominal pain, and blisters or warts.
However, they often cause no pain or other symptoms and therefore go unnoticed.
How can we protect ourselves?
Condoms can reduce the risk of infection, but they do not provide 100% protection.
For some sexually transmitted diseases can also be transmitted by means of contact with infected body fluids.
Therefore, experts recommend regular examinations especially in the case of frequent changes of sexual partners.
Early diagnosis can cure most STIs and prevent long-term complications.

At the age of 136 still had a child
But the most controversial star of the museum is the shepherd Şirali Muslumov, who is said to be 168 years old.

230 Manat (roughly the same amount in euros), Mirzayeva receives monthly as a pension, for local conditions an amount that can live well.

An elk burger is definitely something different. The juicy meat is delicious.
But in the evening the stinky fish is back on the menu.
The hotel where I am staying is one of several venues that will host a Rakfisk dinner where guests can vote for the best - or perhaps the most challenging to the senses - fish.
There is a live TV shot of a fly-covered showman surrounded by plates of raki.
The spectacle is reminiscent of the Eurovision Song Contest.
"What score did you get up there in the mountains for the best fish, Thor-Jürgen?"
"Here are our points, Havard."
People clap and laugh.
A man falls from his chair, possibly overcome by the aquavit.
But perhaps it is the strong smell of all the fish.
Mexico’s Enrique Peña Nieto faces a difficult start
As Mexico’s incoming president Enrique Peña Nieto prepares to take over, Will Grant of the BBC analyses the challenges he faces and the mixed feelings of his people.
Currently, traffic in Mexico City is particularly bad.
Even on better days, this is a congested city, but on Monday a ring of steel was erected to block several major routes into the capital and cause chaos on the roads.
The aim was not to disrupt commuters on their way to work, but to prevent protesters from reaching the Parliament.
On Saturday, Mexico’s new president Enrique Peña Nieto will receive the presidential sash and take over the leadership of the nation.
He is facing a complex task.
Under outgoing President Felipe Calderon, Mexico has been economically successful, but the country is in the grip of a drug war that has already claimed 60,000 lives in the last six years.
"My government is strongly committed to reducing violence," President Peña Nieto told President Barack Obama in the Oval Office earlier this week.
I will propose a new security strategy that will allow us to achieve this goal.
Before he met the US president on his level, Pena Nieto was governor of his home state of Mexico.
In this densely populated, vast part of the country that surrounds the capital, opinions about the new head of state are divided.
A man of action
In the remote little town of Valle del Bravo, for example, they remember him fondly.
The residents of the resort attribute the development of tourism and the construction of infrastructure to him.
To reach the city, you can take one of the highways that Pena Nieto built and that represent a great improvement over the rickety, bumpy roads that used to be here.
Plaque bearing his name also hangs outside a modern sports centre and an impressive interactive museum on climate change.
"We expect him to bring about real and lasting changes," says his friend and political ally Gabriel Olvera Hernandez, who is a PRI congressman.
In particular, as regards security and the economy, we hope for an interesting and real change that our country so badly needs.
After 81 years in power, PRI was replaced in 2000 by Vicente Fox.
The Congresswoman Olvera admits that the party has high expectations for Enrique Peña Nieto after 12 years outside the presidential palace of Los Pinos.
The opposition's accusations that the new president lacks substance he rejects.
He is a very direct man, very committed and has great plans for the country.
He is a great statesman, but he is also someone who can listen.
But on the other side of the state, not many people share this view of their former governor.
In Nezahualcoyotl, also known as Ciudad Neza, the contrast with the paved streets of Valle del Bravo could not be greater.
The place is hidden under highway overpasses and is in many ways a suburb of Mexico City itself.
And the problems in the community are of a fundamentally urban nature.
Earlier this year, the military was called in to combat the drug gangs operating in the neighborhoods, and violence against women is a particularly acute problem.
In a patch of wasteland near a large landfill, dozens of murdered women have been dumped there in the last two years alone.

During Governor Pena Nieto’s term, over 1,000 women were murdered in the state of Mexico - a statistic that even surpasses that of Ciudad Juarez, which is notorious for its violence and the murders of innocent women.
Critics of Pena Nieto believe that he has not adequately addressed the problem of femicide during his tenure.
But in the worst case, his government has been looking the other way.
In a concrete building typical of the run-down neighborhood, Irinea Buendia struggles with tears as she shows me photos of her deceased daughter Mariana Luna.
According to the official version of events, Mariana committed suicide in 2010.
But her family believes she was murdered by her partner.
"When I arrived at her home, it seemed as if her body had been washed," recalls Senora Buendia.
There were signs that she had been beaten, and rigor mortis had already set in.
While her mother tells her story, a picture of Mariana looks down from the wall. It is next to a cross that bears a single word: justice.
But precisely this, the family says, has been denied to it until now.
The authorities have treated me as if I were a blabbermouth, a troublemaker, a nag.
They want to be able to accept their verdict and keep their mouths shut.
"But it is not possible if there were so many irregularities and omissions," she says.
When President Peña Nieto receives the presidential sash on Saturday, he will also assume a great responsibility.
Tens of thousands of Mexican families have been affected by violent crime in the last six years, and the new president has promised to make it a priority during his term.
"I hope as president he will be as he was as governor," says PRI Congressman Olvera in Valle del Bravo.
But it is precisely this fear that the families of the victims in Ciudad Neza are most afraid of.
The prosecution claims that Bradley Manning did not complain about mistreatment
The prosecution disputes Bradley Manning’s claims that he was mistreated in prison
The hearing will address Manning’s time in military custody at Quantico, Virginia
The defence is seeking to have the case dismissed on the grounds of the harsh conditions of detention
The US Army sergeant is accused of stealing thousands of classified documents

On Friday, the prosecution attempted to prove that Army Private Bradley Manning - charged with the biggest leak of classified information in US history - missed several opportunities to complain about the alleged mistreatment he suffered in military custody.

During a pre-trial hearing in Fort Meade, Maryland, Major Ashden Fein stated that records of weekly visits by prison guards during Manning’s nine-month incarceration at Quantico, Virginia, showed no complaints about his treatment.

One day before the trial, which was held at the request of the defence to dismiss the charges - Manning having already been sufficiently punished by his long period of imprisonment - Manning had said he had considered suicide in prison.
The US Army intelligence analyst arrested in June 2010 is accused of stealing thousands of classified documents during his service in Iraq.
The material was then released by WikiLeaks on the internet.
WikiLeaks has never confirmed that Manning was a source of information.

In the hearing on Friday, Fein went through the forms that officials had filled out after their meetings with Manning during his imprisonment at Quantico, where he was held in enhanced conditions from July 2010 to April 2011.
The officers questioned Manning and wrote down his answers.
When Fein asked him on Friday about the forms, Manning admitted that he had rated the treatment by his guards as "excellent" and the treatment by the facility as "very professional."
The forms, so fine, contained no complaints of mistreatment, even though the officials had asked Manning directly about his treatment.
Manning replied that he had expressed his concerns orally and that the officials had discussed them with him and had indicated that they would address them. However, they were not recorded.
"They wrote 'no problems' and that did not necessarily mean I said nothing," says Manning.

Judge Denise Lind asked Manning why he did not complain about his treatment when he met a committee in January 2011 to investigate the suicide thoughts he had mentioned on a form a few months earlier.
Manning replied that his intention during this meeting was to downgrade his observer status to "preventing violations."
The military said it had assigned it this restrictive status - one step below suicide - for its own and for the protection of others.
"I wanted to convince my staff that I was doing well, and to get rid of the monitoring status to achieve a higher quality of life, in my opinion," said Manning.
Manning said on Thursday of his arrest and transfer to Kuwait, where he was held for nearly two months before being transferred to the Marine base at Quantico in Virginia in July 2010.
He said in Kuwait he had considered suicide and had been unconscious due to the heat.
Not knowing what was happening to him or in the outside world was a burden.
"My world shrank to Camp Arafjon, to this cage," said Manning on Thursday.
I thought I was going to die in that cage.
When he was transferred to Quantico, Manning spent most of his days in a small cell - at least 21 hours and often more than 23 hours - and without company.
He was only allowed a mattress, a blanket, flip-flops, clothes and his glasses.
Manning said he had tried to stay on his feet because it was forbidden to sleep or even lie down.
He has always had to sleep in light that has entered his cell from outside.
If he turned around at night and the guards could not see his face, he was woken up to turn around again.
In January 2011, Mannings lawyer formally objected to the treatment of Mannings.
In April 2011, Manning was transferred to the military prison at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

On Friday, Judge Manning also asked about an allegation he made in his testimony on Thursday - that he had to sleep naked in his cell at Quantico and stand naked in front of guards and other prisoners during a morning headcount.
Manning had said that he had never had the opportunity to wrap himself in his blanket during the count.
On Friday, Manning said he had concluded from a guard's order that he should drop the blanket he was wearing, but he admitted that no one had asked him to do so.
On Thursday, Manning said he was forced to sleep naked the previous night. He had tried to show a guard that he was not a threat to himself.
Manning told the officer that he could have used the bond of his underpants or flip-flops to harm himself, but he did not.
In that night, he said, his underwear, flip-flops and glasses were removed from his cell.

His lawyers hope that the judge will at least take into account his experiences in prison and reduce his sentence significantly if he is convicted at his trial before the military court, which is scheduled for early next year.
The defense has said that Manning will plead guilty to lesser offenses while challenging other charges that are deemed too extreme.
The continuation of the hearing is scheduled for this weekend. The Prosecutor is expected to justify the conditions of detention.
The Pentagon remains on its position that Manning was held in accordance with the rules that apply to all detainees held under the highest security at Quantico.

The charges against Manning include aiding the enemy, unauthorized disclosure of intelligence information on the Internet, the transmission of national defense information and the theft of public property or documents.
If he is found guilty on all charges, he faces a life sentence.
My Mexican-American identity crisis.
Many people are forced to leave Mexico because of the lack of opportunities
Mexicans tend to blame the emigrants - they recall the hard times
Navarrette believes that Mexican Americans are caught between two worlds
On a recent trip to Mexico City, I had just walked through the hall and was at the passport control when I felt a sense of bewilderment.
Signs pointed to two lines: one for "Mexicanos" ("Mexicans"), the other for "Extranjeros" ("foreigners").
I stood there for a few seconds, unsure which way to go.
I grew up in central California and was called a "Mexican" all my life.
An ethnic label - just as my friends in Boston call themselves "Irish" or my friends in New York call themselves "Italian."
Later I decided to go for "Mexican-American".
But this was Mexico.
And in my grandfather's home there was no need for abbreviations or hyphens.
I was just an American.
I speak Spanish, at least well enough to hold my own in an interview at either end of the language.
But I do not have the vocabulary of a native speaker, and I will not be able to shake off my American accent.
So I took my American passport and stood in line for Extranjeros.
I thought about that moment this week when the future President of Mexico, Enrique Peña Nieto, visited the White House to meet with President Obama.
The agenda included all the topics that one would expect to see on the agenda of these two countries: immigration, drugs and trade.
Nieto was also very keen to talk about the growth of the Mexican economy. It is one of the reasons why Mexicans are now more likely to stay in Mexico rather than emigrate to the United States.
He wants to join forces with the United States and Canada to create a North American trading bloc modelled on the European Union.
And Pena Nieto vowed to continue Mexico’s war on drug cartels, even if he did not provide details.
Mexico’s relationship with the United States is complicated and fraught with resentment.
Most Americans probably never give a thought to the fact that the United States invaded Mexico in 1848 and forced the country’s leadership to cede more than half of its territory to them.
But for Mexicans who think in centuries and not in minutes, memories of this event cannot be overlooked.
As soon as any US government official criticizes Mexico, there is a chorus of complaints in Mexican media and among the country's elites about how the Americans are encroaching on their sovereignty.
And the children of Montezuma embark on a path of war.
And yet Mexico’s greatest challenge is in fact in its relationship with the more than 35 million Mexican Americans living in the United States.
Lust to talk about resentments?
There is more than enough.
Mexico has winners and losers. People for whom the country offers opportunities, and others for whom it does not.

The only reason why so many people of Mexican origin live in cities like Los Angeles, Las Vegas, Phoenix, Denver or San Antonio is because at some point in our lineage, a person - perhaps a parent or grandparent - was denied a chance in Mexico and migrated north.
And in most cases, this person matched a profile - dark-skinned, uneducated, from a poor village, etc.
We are the descendants of these people, and our loyalty is to them.
Not Mexico.
And even though we may now be living the American dream, having attended good schools and having good jobs, we must never lose sight of the American dream - not the Mexican dream.
Our identity is sometimes blurred, but our loyalty is not.
This is clearly the United States.
Moreover, we are aware that many members of the Mexican elite do not like us.
This is based on reciprocity.
They see us as a monument to a humiliating defeat and look down on us because we are not Mexican enough.
Our Spanish will never be good enough, our band to Mexico will never be strong enough.
In your opinion, our existence is a symbol of failure.
If our families had not failed in Mexico, they would not have left.
And then we would not be trapped behind the veil - with a pleasant life in the United States, but somehow lost.

My wife, who was born in Guadalajara and who immigrated legally to the United States as a child, reminds me that there are tensions between Mexicans and Mexican Americans because Mexicans have a clearer sense of who they are - and Mexican Americans resent that.
While she is an American citizen, she sees herself as part of two countries.
But many Mexican Americans I know feel they do not belong to either country.
We love the Mexican band Los Tigres del Norte, but also Bruce Springsteen.
It enjoys the best of both worlds, but is rooted in neither.
In Mexico we are seen as Americans.
And in the United States we are seen as Mexicans.

As I learned during my travels, there is something that makes this relationship even more complicated: some Mexican leaders and parts of the educated class want to re-establish their ties with the diaspora.
They want to use Mexican Americans as temporary "ambassadors" to represent their interests in the United States.
We should tell our American colleagues how great a visit to this country is and put pressure on the political leadership to strengthen ties with Mexico.
Now.
That will not happen.
Too many wounded feelings.
And given the unfair distribution of income, the rampant corruption and the drug violence, many of us are not so sure that it is really a great country.
I fear that you will have to do this alone, amigos.
That is fair.

If at least some Mexicans are not yet ready to forgive the United States for its treatment of Mexico 150 years ago, they must also accept that some Mexican Americans harbor a grudge against their family members who were treated badly not so long ago.
Hmm.
Perhaps we are "Mexican" than I thought.
Old battles, new Middle East
The ceasefire between Israel and Hamas could prove to be an unexpected cornerstone of peace
Can there ever be lasting peace between Arabs and Jews in the Middle East?
The latest bloody events seem to snuff out such hope.

Amidst the usual finger-pointing, countless buildings were reduced to rubble, more than 140 Palestinians, most of them civilians, and six Israelis were killed - and for the first time rockets from Gaza struck near the Israeli metropolis of Tel Aviv and the holy city of Jerusalem.
Yet, despite the historical conflict between Israelis and Palestinians, the Middle East around them is changing.
The Arab Spring has created a new, uncertain situation, and whether they like it or not - Palestinians and Israelis are part of the turmoil.
This may only lead to more bloodshed.
But there are reasons to believe that the deadly deadlock could finally come to an end.
A war that is neither won nor lost
At first glance, optimism in the face of the current situation seems to be out of place.
Even if the ceasefire agreed on November 21 holds, the fighting of the past week has hardened the hardliners on both sides.
The leaders of Hamas, the Islamic movement that has controlled the Gaza Strip since 2007, will claim to have pushed back the Israelis, even though its group has suffered great losses.

Despite the fact that several Hamas leaders have been killed and 1.7 million Gazans are trapped in one of the most desolate and densely populated corners of the planet, Israel has not been able to destroy Hamas.
In fact, Hamas is gaining ground in the West Bank, which is controlled by the rival moderate Palestinian group Fatah.
And the Hamas leaders could conclude that they have the time on their side.
Thus, as Islamists have gained influence in the Arab world, Hamas has been able to attract powerful and wealthy friends.
Turkey, a resurgent regional power once considered Israel's closest Muslim ally, has taken sides with Hamas - as has Qatar, one of the wealthiest and most dynamic Gulf states.

Jubilant Hamas supporters believe that an Islamic crescent is forming around Israel - from Lebanon in the north, where the militant Hezbollah has the power, to Syria, where rebels of an increasingly Islamic bent may be poised to topple Bashar al-Assad, to Jordan, where Hamas allies threaten the king.

And in particular, the rise of the Muslim Brotherhood under President Muhammad Morsi in Egypt - the most populous and important Arab country - on the southern flank of Israel has fundamentally changed the balance of the region.
Hosni Mubarak, the secular despot who ruled Egypt for 30 years until his overthrow in 2011, had little time for Hamas.
In contrast, the Brotherhood is tied to Hamas and its leaders are more dependent on popular sentiment.
In future diplomatic negotiations, Hamas could emerge as an actor that cannot be excluded from the equation by Israel and the United States.
Israeli hardliners, on the other hand, draw the opposite conclusion.
Militarily speaking, Hamas is no longer a threat.
Israel's missile defense system, "Iron Dome," has proven itself and many of the rockets have been destroyed.
Israel will be able to sleep more peacefully for a while.
In diplomatic terms, the United States has remained steadfast in its position. Many European countries have blamed Hamas for the latest escalations of violence.
Israel has done well in recent years, especially under Prime Minister Binyamin Netanyahu, who has largely ignored the peace process.

Although rockets from the Gaza Strip have killed about 30 Israelis since 2004, the country has remained relatively free of suicide bombers - not least thanks to the barriers that have been built in the West Bank, which is the main part of any future Palestinian state. These protect the Jewish settlements, which have been declared illegal but have been expanding.
Netanyahu is doing well. His Likud party has allied itself with an even more combative group ahead of the January 22 elections.
Why should we also pamper these crafty Palestinians and give them their own state?
If they actually had control of the West Bank, wouldn’t they also fire rockets at Israel, just like their brethren in Gaza?
No, it is better to keep them behind the wall and punish them if they dare to raise their heads.
The hardliners may prevail. But the Arab Spring could upset their plans.
Even if the Islamists who now rule Egypt and other countries have little love for Israel, they will first focus on the difficulties in their own countries.
Israel’s defense budget is larger than the combined defense budgets of its four Arab neighbors.
A war with the local superpower will not help the new Arab governments to rebuild their economies.
That President Morsi met with Barack Obama to reach a ceasefire could be a promising sign - and perhaps the beginning of a new era.
Israelis should also think long-term.

While the rest of the Arab world is taking tentative steps towards democratization, Palestinians continue to be denied their right to self-determination - a powder keg that will undoubtedly explode one day in the Israeli-occupied territories, just as a bus exploded in Tel Aviv this week.
The repression is already undermining the democracy of the Jewish state, and with the growth of the Arab population, this situation will only become worse.
Bloody missions to push the Hamas out of Gaza will increasingly demand a diplomatic price over the years.
Both sides need an external stimulus

The right answer is the one that is being given by the more reasonable representatives of both sides, by the majority of the rest of the world and by this newspaper: two states, one of which is Israel, which will have to give up territory for security reasons.
The - for the near future small - hope is that the ceasefire will give outsiders more influence to enforce this solution.

Egypt must now, together with Turkey and Qatar, stop arms supplies to the Gaza Strip and is better placed than ever to convince Hamas of the idea of a Jewish state based on the 1967 borders, supplemented by land swaps and a shared Jerusalem.
Arab nations outside should also encourage Hamas and Fatah to reach an agreement.
That would be more done for the creation of a Palestinian state than with the forthcoming application for UN observer status.
Obama too must do his part to bring Israel to the negotiating table.
During his first term, he failed to present his own peace plan.
Far away in the White House it seems as if he is also reluctant to commit.
But that is a regrettable, short-sighted perspective.
The United States has a vital interest in a stable Middle East.
And this includes a peace agreement between Israel and the Palestinians.
Australian laws on uniform cigarette packaging come into force
Health warnings and diseased body parts on neutral green packaging, which are the same for all tobacco brands

The world’s first uniform packaging laws for cigarettes and tobacco have come into force in Australia. They will replace brand logos and colours with neutral olive green caps, which will also be printed with stark images of diseased bodies and babies and children affected by smoking.

Apart from the different health warnings and pictures, the only difference between the packs in the brand names, which are printed in identical, small print, is that the new packs will have a new logo.
This makes Australia the world leader in tobacco packaging regulation.
The Australian Federal Government wants to discourage young people from smoking by removing the glamorous image of tobacco use.
The government is basing its policy on studies showing that people who have not started smoking by age 26 are 99% unlikely to start later.

"We can see that even young children understand the message that tobacco companies are trying to convey through their brand image," said Federal Health Minister Tanya Plibersek. She cites studies that have shown, for example, that children associate a crown with the idea of a princess.

Although Australia has one of the lowest smoking rates in the world and the changes will have little impact on the profits of multinational corporations, other countries are already considering similar steps.
The tobacco lobby fought hard against the laws.
It was said that the laws would encourage black-market trade, leading to cheaper and more readily available cigarettes.
"The laws will lead to serious unintended consequences," says Scott McIntyre of British American Tobacco Australia.
Chinese and Indonesian counterfeiters will be selling much larger quantities of these products on the streets of Australia.
Others say that the laws have helped to boost their business.

Sandra Ha of Zico Import Pty Ltd, a small family business, notes that demand for cigarette cases and silicone covers to cover the unpalatable packaging has soared since the big tobacco companies British American Tobacco, Britain's Imperial Tobacco, Philip Morris and Japan Tobacco lost their challenge to the laws in the top Australian court two months ago.
Zico has sold up to 6,000 units to wholesalers and is waiting for new stock.
For us, it is a good business.
Experts say the hook is in the popularity of social media among the very group the plan is aimed at.

A number of Australian laws have banned tobacco companies from TV advertising, prohibited them from being sports sponsors and forced most retailers to stop selling cigarettes in shops. Now tobacco advertising has moved online.
The Australian government has banned online advertising by local businesses and sites, but has no control over international sites.
"Who markets tobacco and has only a small area to promote their products, can't get around the internet," says Becky Freeman, a health researcher at the University of Sydney.
On social media sites like YouTube, Twitter and Facebook, Freeman has seen an increase in user-generated reviews of brands written by "ordinary people."
The question is: is this just a private person who is so fond of Marlboro cigarettes that she even makes a video about it - or is it a marketing agency?
British American Tobacco Australia says the industry is focusing on compliance rather than marketing.

It has even gone so far as to pay Ukraine, Honduras and the Dominican Republic to challenge the new rules - those countries complain to the World Trade Organisation about unfair trade restrictions, even though none of the countries trade more with Australia than with any other country.
A WTO decision is expected by mid-2013.
Plibersek says that the government has been talking to other countries that are considering similar packaging laws.
Canada was the first country to require photographic warnings in 2001.
They have now been extended to more than 40 countries, including Brazil, Turkey and Ukraine.
Stricter laws are being considered in the UK, New Zealand, South Africa and India.
Many Australian smokers are defiant.
The images do not affect me.
I simply ignore them.
"You just take a cigarette and put the pack away," says Victor El Hage as he buys a cigarette pack bearing a photo of a mouth tumor.
Frankly, there is only one reason why I would stop, and that is my little girl.
James Yu, operator of the King of the Pack tobacco shop in Sydney's CBD, says the uniform packaging has made it harder to stock his shelves.
"Before I used to take an hour to sort out a delivery, now I need four hours," says Yu.
"The government should have just banned cigarettes completely - then we would have said okay, that's it, we're closing down," he says, visibly angry.
In a constantly electrified world it is nice to be bored sometimes
This Thanksgiving I spent an unexpected five hours at the airport, as our plane was grounded due to mechanical problems and we had to wait for another plane.
I had plenty of time to think about boredom.
I will not lie.
Waiting for a half day at the airport for a flight is pretty nerve-wracking - even if books, magazines and iPhones (and of course tax-free shopping) are available.
But more and more academics and child development experts are promoting boredom as something positive.
If it is up to them, it is okay for us - and our children - to be bored sometimes.
This forces the brain to get lost in interesting thought processes, which may foster creativity.
And because most of us stare at one or another screen almost constantly these days, the benefits of boredom no longer apply to us.
Should we welcome boredom with open arms?
Yes.
And no.
I will come back to this point.
Like many people I have always assumed boredom is a relatively recent phenomenon that has developed with increasing leisure time.
But Peter Toohey, professor of Greek and Roman history at the University of Calgary in Canada and author of Boredom: A Lively History (Yale University Press, 2011) sees it differently.
"In fact boredom has a very long history," he says.
Pompeii’s domestic walls are decorated with a Latin graffiti about boredom dating from the first century.
And then there is the question of how we actually define boredom.
According to John D. Eastwood, an associate professor of psychology at the University of York in Ontario, Canada, the problem is that boredom has been defined and discussed in many different ways.

After much reading of research literature and presenting the idea to a focus group of about 100 people, Professor Eastwood and his colleagues concluded that boredom can be defined as the experience of wanting to do something satisfying but not being able to do it.
Boredom differs from apathy in that the person is not engaged in what he or she would like to be doing.
Apathy, on the other hand, is a lack of drive to do anything.
The key experience of boredom, he says, is a "disruption of the process of attention, combined with bad mood and the feeling that time is passing slowly".
Boredom can almost sound like depression.
But Professor Eastwood believes, although these two conditions may be related, bored people see the problem in their environment or in the world, while depressed people see the problem in themselves.
Sometimes we think we are bored, even though we are just having difficulty concentrating.

In their study "The Unengaged Mind: Defining Boredom in Terms of Attention" - in German, for example, "The Unengaged Mind: Defining Boredom in Terms of Attention" - which appeared in the September issue of the journal "Perspectives on Psychological Science" - Professor Eastwood and his colleagues point to an earlier experiment in which participants listened to a tape in which a person read a magazine article.

Some groups heard a loud TV program from the neighboring room, which had nothing to do with the content. Others heard it at a low volume, so it was barely audible, while the third group heard it not at all.

The people who heard the barely audible television said they felt more bored than the other two groups - they had trouble concentrating, could not find a reason for this and wrote their difficulties down to boredom.

When trying to focus on a difficult or strenuous task, the disruption of attention can lead to boredom, says Mark J. Fenske, an associate professor of neuroscience at the University of Guelph in Ontario and one of the authors of the study.
If, on the other hand, you are engaged in a monotonous activity - "like searching for defective products on a factory conveyor belt, music can distract and help you not to feel bored".
Indeed, he says, we now know that fidgeting and doodling, often interpreted as signs of boredom, can actually combat it by making people more attentive.
"Studies have shown that children who are allowed to toddle around learn more and retain more information than those who are forced to sit still," says Professor Fenske.
We all get bored at some point - my delayed flight, a droning speaker, a particularly boring film.
But some people get bored more easily than others.
To measure these differences, researchers in the 1980s developed a "scale of boredom susceptibility".
The scale includes statements such as "Many things I have to do are repetitive and monotonous" and "I have so many interests that I do not have enough time for everything".
Using such scales, researchers have found that boys get bored more often than girls - especially in terms of the need for more and a wider variety of external stimuli.
But in general, teenagers are a pretty stressed-out bunch.

In 1991, Reed Larson, a professor of human and community development at the University of Illinois, conducted an experiment in which he contacted nearly 400 teenagers and their parents seven to eight times a day via pager.
He found that 32% of young people were bored in school and doing homework, while 23% said they were bored when they were not in school.
Yet only 3% of parents said they felt bored.
Professor Larson says today, 21 years later, he does not know if the percentages of boredom have increased or decreased.
He is, however, certain that "youth is perceived as particularly boring" mainly because children and teenagers have little influence over their daily lives.
So, back to my original question: is boredom healthy?
Sometimes not, because in the extreme it leads people to take extreme physical risks and to become addicted to gambling or drugs - studies have shown this.

On the other hand, many philosophers and authors are studying the relationship between boredom and creativity. This is the opinion of Professor Vodanovich, who has been researching the subject for more than two decades.
"With boredom, the brain is telling you to do something else," says Gary Marcus, a psychology professor at New York University.
But the brain does not always know what to do best.
If you get bored and use that energy to play guitar and cook, you will be happy.
But television can provide short-term pleasure, but it can also be a source of long-term disappointment.
If you give your bored child an iPad, it will distract it from boredom. But it will not learn to entertain itself or control itself, says Professor Fenske.
And he adds: "Self-regulation is transferred from one situation to another".
The child not only learns to communicate, but also gains greater self-control in other areas.
I do not believe that we should celebrate boredom.
We should also not be too critical of them.
Instead, our goal should be to feel comfortable in our own skin, even away from the constant barrage of activity and technology.
Professor Eastwood agrees.
"It sounds as if we should be bored more often. But boredom is the tormenting, relentless desire to do something meaningful," he says.
He believes that people are really looking for a way to switch off and relax.
"In an environment where we are constantly overstimulated, it is difficult to engage when the noise has died down."
In Colorado there is no clear guideline for the new marijuana law

The 19-year-old community college student and football player Anthony Orozco is facing a court hearing in southeastern Colorado for a crime that will soon be legal in the state: the possession of a few scraps of marijuana and a pipe to smoke it.
According to Orozco and some friends, they were driving in a car on a September day in Lamar near the Kansas border when they were stopped.

After the police officer found marijuana in the car, Orozco was summoned to court for possession of drugs and drug paraphernalia - minor offenses each carrying a $100 fine - and was given a court date.
"We will be treated like criminals," says Orozco.
But is he also one?
In the uncertain weeks after the state’s decision to legalize small amounts of marijuana for personal use, the answer to hundreds of minor drug offenses depends less on the law than on the location.
Hundreds of marijuana-related infractions have already been dropped here and in Washington state, where similar measures have been approved.
Police authorities will no longer prosecute adults over 21 for possession of small amounts. This will be legalised as the new laws come into force in the coming weeks.
But prosecutors in more conservative parts of Colorado have announced that they will continue to prosecute existing marijuana offenses and are still citing people in court.
At the same time, several cities, from the suburbs of Denver to the Western Mountains, vote to prevent new state-licensed marijuana businesses from opening in their communities.
"This situation is developing so rapidly that I don't even know what's going to happen next," says Daniel J. Oates, police chief in Aurora, which is east of Denver.
And regulators in the state of Washington are scratching their heads in bewilderment.
They are waiting for guidance on setting up a licensing system for the production, manufacture, distribution and sale of the drug - and have a deadline of 1 December 2013 in mind.

In Washington, it is believed that Colorado is in any case ahead of most states in terms of regulating marijuana. There, the drug was legalized first for medical use and then for personal consumption.
"Colorado has a more regulated market. It is therefore a good place to look for guidance," says Brian E. Smith, spokesman for the Washington State Liquor Control Board.
But Smith also acknowledges that no place or system can do more than serve as a rough guide.
"We have no real precedent to follow," he adds.
The Washington law, called I-502, takes effect on December 6, thus ending a gray area in which the state licensing system does not exist but possession is legal.

And unpleasant practical questions need to be resolved at this time - for example, how to reconcile the state's requirement of "appropriate access" to licensed marijuana with the prohibition of cannabis businesses within 300 metres of schools, parks, playgrounds and childcare facilities.

"It will be harder to find a location for a licensed cannabis business than in urban areas, especially in the urban areas of Seattle," says Ben Livingston, spokesman for the Center for Legal Cannabis, a recently formed research group.

On November 21, Chief Oates sent an email to Aurora employees stating that the prosecutor would no longer prosecute minor marijuana offenses for people over 21, and that the police would no longer file charges for these offenses.
Chief Oates added that the police would continue to enforce local regulations on medical marijuana growers and drug dealers would continue to be prosecuted.
In Weld County in northern Colorado, District Attorney Ken Buck takes a more stringent view.
After the vote, he said that his agency would continue to pursue cases of marijuana possession, mainly to encourage users to quit.
Currently, 119 people are facing trial for possession of less than 50 grams of marijuana, even though many of them have been charged with other crimes.
"Our agency has a duty to investigate violations of the law that were crimes at the time they were committed," Buck said in a statement.
The reactions are mixed even in places like rural Mesa County, where voters rejected the marijuana initiative,
The police in Grand Junction, the county’s largest city, no longer arrest adults for possession of small amounts.
District Attorney Pete Hautzinger supported this decision, but also decided not to drop all pending property forfeiture cases.
"I do not believe that I am wasting my time enforcing the law until it changes," he says.

Although 55% of voters in Colorado supported the measure, it was clear from the beginning that it would not be easy to reconcile personal consumption of marijuana with the complexities of government and the legal system.
And the contradictory reactions across the country fostered a deep division among local officials about the big green experiment.

District attorneys are a "cultural barrier," says Sean McAllister, a Denver attorney who represents marijuana defendants in court and serves as a spokesman for the national organization that advocates for marijuana law reform.
"They have spent such a large part of their lives prosecuting people for having the courage to accept the legalisation," he believes.
As the first states to treat small amounts of marijuana like alcohol, Colorado and Washington are being touted as national models for the legalization of drugs.

While advocates and officials prepare for a legal era of sales, they are also nervously awaiting instructions from the federal government, which continues to treat the sale and cultivation of marijuana as a crime.
Supporters of the legalization movement hope that the Justice Ministry will give in.

Despite several high-profile arrests of consumers and sellers of medical marijuana, the federal government has largely allowed the sale of medical marijuana in Colorado, Washington, and 16 other states.

Kevin A. Sabet, a former drug policy adviser to the Obama administration, believes that law enforcement officers will probably not enter to seize small amounts of drugs, but will probably resist allowing legal, state-regulated marijuana businesses to operate under the new legislation.
Several cities in Colorado are waiting for the federal government to act.
Before the election, some local governments approved moratoriums on new marijuana shops, even though they would not open for another year.
Last week, Montrose, a town in the west, voted to ban it for six months, which is likely to be approved next week.
"We do not want to get into a position where we license someone and then have a big problem at the federal level," said Bob Nicholson, a member of the City Council.
Our community voted against this legislative change.
We are guided by what the community has chosen and not by what the state has chosen.
There are still many questions to be answered.
Petronella Wyatt: I was bullied at Oxford because I am a Tory
Not only are university students today being attacked for their views
It has always been my greatest dream to be given a place at the University of Oxford.

Both my father and my older brother had attended the university that I once considered to be the greatest temple of knowledge in the world, a modern Greek symposium that promoted the great pillars of civilization - free thought and tolerance.
But within two weeks of moving into Worcester College at the end of the 1980s - where I had intended to study history - I had packed my bags again and thus brought about the first scandal of my life.
My father broke down in tears.
My friends were confused.
The Evening Standard said I had left because I had a problem with my fellow students having sex in the room next door.
The author A N Wilson joked that I had left the university because I was forced to drink from damaged cups.
The truth was less amusing.
I ran away.
Yes, I ran because I was being subjected to systematic harassment and threats.
Not because of my rather unusual name, or because I came from a private school.

I was persecuted for only one reason - a reason that seemed even more narrow-minded and cruel in this supposed cradle of enlightenment: my late father, Woodrow Wyatt, had been a key adviser to Margaret Thatcher and I was a supporter of the Conservative Party.
Why am I mentioning this now?
Well, according to current reports, a new generation of moderate-right students is also under similar persecution.

The organized and rising hatred of Tory students in Oxford has now reached such a level that a group of them last week called for the same equality protection that is given to gays, the disabled and ethnic minorities.
Conservative members of the Junior Common Room (JCR) of Corpus Christi College claim to be "often actively isolated, personally attacked and made to feel unwelcome" because of their political views.
They demand a seat on their college’s committee for equal representation, to ensure that their views can be expressed freely.
Their situation was exacerbated by a recent documentary on political students on BBC Two, "Wonderland: Young, Bright and on the Right", which portrayed Tories as eccentric and neo-Nazi.
Among those shown was graduate Joe Cooke, former president of the Conservative Union at Oxford, who drove a Rolls-Royce and strutted around in silver suit and silver walking stick.
At other universities, conservative students say they are being treated as "scapegoats for the introduction of higher tuition fees."
Luke Black, 20, vice-president of the Conservative Students' Association at Nottingham University, was quoted in a Sunday newspaper as saying: "There is a growing left-wing tendency on campuses.
People think we are like the Bullingdon Club, without having even met us.

Samuel Roberts, 21 and a history student at Corpus Christi, who initiated the request for greater protection, believes such an atmosphere is "uncomfortable". The 19-year-old Stephanie Cherill, the newly appointed president of the Conservative Association of Oxford Students, says she has observed a growing rejection of moderate right-wing students among JCR members.
"This is a threat to intellectual discourse and to the well-being of the members," she says.
In my first weeks in Oxford I was part of such a minority.
As an incredibly shy 18-year-old, I arrived in September 1986.
The hatred of the Conservative Party had reached its peak.
Last year, the University voted to deny an honorary degree to Margaret Thatcher, a former student, due to the cuts in higher education.
The atmosphere would have even made Stalinists wince.
During the first days of the first semester, when new students and tutors get to know each other, I got a taste of what was to come.
I have experienced tutors tolerating and even participating in the mocking of Tory students.
Political issues such as the miners' strike, privatization and the government's rejection of sanctions against the apartheid regime found their way into the wooden-panelled rooms of the tutorial.
At my first one of these events I was asked to translate French texts from the 18th century into English. I was not prepared for what was to come.
"Miss Wyatt," said Harry Pitt (who died later), "please translate the first paragraph."
I stumbled over it.
Pitt was a small man with a face like a piece of cake, and rather nasty.
"Do Thatcher supporters refuse to learn French, or are they just stupid?", he asked me.
The other students laughed.
In my opinion tears were flowing.
"I suggest that you take a few French lessons in your spare time - so long as you're not too busy with your social activities," Pitt grumbled.
I returned to my room with my head hanging.
That evening I was alone in the college dining hall having dinner when someone tapped me on the shoulder.
It was a second-year English student named James who introduced himself as a member of the Conservative Student Association.
"I know who you are," he said, in a friendly way.
Unfortunately, it is as it is.
Anyone suspected of being Tory is persecuted.
For me it is bad enough, but they know that your father is close to Margaret Thatcher, so it will be worse for you.
Most Tory first-years claim to be Labour supporters.
Later, in a local pub, I tried to pass myself off as a local.
I insisted that I did not agree with Mrs Thatcher on all points.
This trick should prove to be a failure.
A first-year student in Philosophy, Politics and Economics, who ironically attended the conservative Eton College, said to me: "You are the daughter of a fascist pig".
You are polluted.
Other students shared his opinion.
I was perverse and dirty.
"How do Tories have sex?" asked one.
They are fighting each other, right?
I felt as homosexuals must have felt before the more liberal legislation of the United States.
Would I ever be able to lead a normal life at the University of Oxford?
Would I be able to meet like-minded people only after the darkness had fallen?
Should I turn to the Labour Party and suppress my natural inclinations?
The three years that lay before me stretched out in my mind's eye to a place of ostracism and exile.
The only tutor who openly declared himself a Tory was Norman Stone, Professor of Contemporary History, who was based in my college.
He was not only hated for being a conservative, but also for advising her on foreign policy and writing speeches for her.
He was rarely there.
He hated the place, found it provincial and petty-minded, and rejected it for its Marxist-deterministic view of history.
In 1997 he took up a professorship at Bilkent University in Ankara, Turkey.
"You will not be happy here," he said to me.
I began to commute between Oxford and my parents' home and found refuge with more open-minded friends and family members in the city.
I told my father that I hated Oxford and why I did.
He seemed incredulous.
During his time in the 1940s, all political views were accepted.
"But it is the best place in the world," he said quietly.
They would never do something like that, not in my city of dreaming spires.
Even my Communist friends were always well-mannered.
His eyes were moist.
Give it a chance.
I am sure they are just teasing you.
I would break my heart if you left.
Exhausted by my frequent trips to London, my emotional resistance weakened.
One of my male friends, also a Tory supporter, had succumbed to the pressure and abandoned his convictions.
During a tutorial the following week, in which another history tutor seriously claimed that I was "an enemy of the people", I decided to do the same.
Although I secretly felt ashamed, I admitted that my parents had brainwashed me, calling them "old fools".
The relief was short-lived.
It was my father who nailed the last nail in the coffin of my Oxford career.
At that time he wrote two columns a week in Murdoch’s press.
My door was locked.
I hid in my room, and after five minutes my guards gave up.
As they left, I packed a suitcase and took the first train to London.
I never returned.
I am happy to be called a 'slap-happy' man.
But no 18-year-old should ever have to suffer such intimidation and nastiness in an educational institution.
And even more tragic is that it was Oxford - a university that not only produced 14 Tory Prime Ministers but has, to date, hidden behind an undeserved reputation for equality and freedom of thought.
"Valentino prefers celebrity elegance"

On the occasion of the exhibition "Valentino - Master of Couture" which opened this week in London, ABC talks to Naty Abascal, Fiona Thyssen-Bornemisza and other famous clients of the Italian fashion designer.
Somerset House, the former residence of Queen Elizabeth I of England, is the only place in the British capital worthy of hosting an exhibition about Valentino Garavani.

This was acknowledged by the designer at the opening of "Valentino - Master of Couture", a magnificent retrospective, which brings together more than 130 dresses created by his "Maison" over the last 50 years.
"I love this palace," he says with his unmistakable Italian accent.
This exhibition is the culmination of a story whose only protagonist is "il signore" Garavani, but which could not have been written without his distinguished clientele.
Valentino has always been fascinated by the stuffy and distant world of the aristocracy.

In the first room of this exhibition, which will be on display until 3 March, there is a wealth of private letters and photographs signed by the most distinguished aristocracy, starting with Princess Salimah Aga Khan, through Princess Marie-Chantal of Greece and Margarita of England to Lord Snowdon.
Valentino shows these personal memories as trophies of his social ascent from modest fashion designer in the town of Voghera in northern Italy to the idol of the international jet set.
To be in love with the nobility need not be a disadvantage.
"At least they don't leave their butts on your beautiful carpet, as some famous pop stars do," says Baroness Fiona Thyssen-Bornemisza.
In the 60's and 70's they lived in the Alps and were good friends.
Valentino is a spectacular, generous and elegant host.
"We all enjoyed being invited to his home in Gstaad", says the ex-wife of "Heini" Thyssen, who is close friends with forgotten beauties like Marella Agnelli or Eugenie Niarchos.
Valentino has always preferred the elegance of celebrity.
And yet he is a star.
Valeria Mazza, in a Valentino dress
The Argentinean model Valeria Mazza also does not forget the charisma of the fashion designer.
Many years ago we went to dinner with him at his home after a fashion show at the Piazza di Spagna in Rome.
We were about 20 people, including Sharon Stone and John Kennedy Jr.
In every detail of his apartment, the decoration, the food and the music you could feel his influence.
"All the guests felt important and loved", recalls the "Top Model" who began her career at the Haute Couture Week in Paris in 1995.
"It never goes out of fashion because his designs are works of art" she concludes.
Fashion show of origin
Garavani’s life is not a story of obsession, but rather of mutual love affairs.
He may be a man of good education and the highest titles, and they love him.

One of the galleries in Somerset House has been transformed into a glorious and 60-metre-long catwalk, suggesting a role reversal: the user takes the place of the model and walks along the catwalk to admire a dreamlike "audience" of masterpieces by Valentino, such as the dress that Jackie Kennedy chose for her wedding to Aristóteles Onassis, the costumes worn by Monica Vitti in La Notte, or a coat in wool and leather that belonged to the Empress Farah Diba.
In this audience of fashion dolls shine names such as that of Sibilla de Luxemburgo, Gloria von Thurn and Taxis, Mette-Marit of Norway, Rosario of Bulgaria or Sofia of Habsburg.
Naty Abascal and the fashion designer, 2006
Many of these women say that the first Valentino is like the first love, "unforgettable".
I can remember perfectly well.
It was a trouser, a shirt, a waistcoat type "Gillette" and a jacket from the autumn/winter collection 1971-1972.
"It was a gift from him," says Naty Abascal, one of the designer's muses.
"I prefer him to all the others because he loves women and because he enhances our beauty," says the ex-duchess of Feria.
I like the colors he uses very much; they have a lot of light and highlight the face.
The proportions are perfect.
The Princess and fashion leader Patricia della Giovampaola d'Arenberg can not forget the first time she wore a Valentino.
When I was a teenager living in Italy, I dreamed of finally having the age and opportunity to wear one of its evening dresses...
In the late 1990s, it finally happened.
I bought my first Valentino dress for a party at my cousin's castle, Prince Edouard de Ligne.
It was a red dress with a flowing skirt and a draped bodice that is worthy of its name.
"It was a dream come true," says the widow of Rodrigo d'Arenberg.
"Valentino is not dependent on fashion, his obsession is timeless," explains this Italian aristocrat who lives between Paris, New York and Buenos Aires.
The Princess D'Arenberg preserves her evening dresses by the fashion designer "with absolute care", "because a dress is not only a dress but also the memories associated with it".
The "King" of fashion
The grand finale of the exhibition at Somerset House is Marie-Chantal Miller’s wedding dress for her wedding to Pablo de Grecia in 1995.

Four months of work and 25 "ragazze" (as the designer called his seamstresses) were needed to make this ivory silk dress with pearls, twelve different embroideries and a four and a half meter long train.

According to the journalist Suzy Menkes, the top authority in the fashion press, this dress was a milestone in haute couture at the end of the 20th century, "the return to the clientele of the upper classes".
For years tainted by the "savoir-être" of the elite, Valentino is now its best example.

Knight of the Grand Cross (the highest honour in Italy), Knight of the Order of the Lavoro, Commander of the Order of Arts and Letters, awarded the Legion of Honour, Garavani has as many honours as any of his clients' husbands.
"I have always admired his refinement, his calm, his well-groomed and perfect appearance," says D'Arenberg.
I saw him last month at a gala dinner in the Orsay Museum.
He was sitting at the table of the Countess Jacqueline de Ribes, a very good friend of mine.
"He was flawless; time leaves no mark on him".
And this is what a princess says...
The world’s most difficult job: the human beasts of Kawah Ijen
For four euros, the carriers of the Indonesian volcano carry 70 kilos of sulfur over the steep, rocky paths.
There are people for whom their work is hell, and there are people who literally work in hell.
This is the case of Anto Wijaya, one of the 400 miners who earn their living by extracting sulphur from the Kawah Ijen volcano in East Java.
To do this, he must go down every day to the bottom of his crater, where the sulphur-containing gas that is emitted from the earth is solidified in contact with the air.
After he has extracted large sulfur stones, which can weigh up to 70 kilos, he carries them in two bamboo baskets on his shoulders over the steep stone paths.

It is only 250 metres to the top of the volcano, which rises to a height of 2386 metres, but the exhausted carriers need more than 40 minutes to reach the summit at a tortoise pace, having to maintain their balance and take their steps carefully so as not to slip and fall.
You know that every step can cost your life, as it happened to a French tourist who fell to her death on the steep slopes of the Kawah Ijen a few years ago.
The miners of Kawah Ijen earn 5 cents for every kilo of sulfur they extract.

Once there, they make their way between the tourists who photograph them like circus animals and walk three kilometres to the scale, which a mining company has set up a little further down at an altitude of 1850 metres

The company is PT Candi Ngrimbi, which since 1960 has exploited the deposits in the volcano and (never better said) its workers, to which it pays 662 Indonesian rupiahs (5 euro cents) per kilo of sulphur.
It sells it for 10,000 rupees (83 cents) to the petrochemical industry because it is widely used in everyday life, for making matches, fireworks, cosmetics, dynamite and even bleaching sugar.
"As we normally carry 70 kg, we get for each trip approximately 46,000 rupees (3.8 euro) ", explains Anto, who normally does three trips a day.
For each trip he needs three hours, after which he is completely exhausted, but at the end of the day he has 138,000 rupees (11.5 euros) together.
What looks like a miserable wage for such a grueling effort is actually three times what he would earn from working the fields.

"The daily wage of the miners here, where during the coffee harvest 15,000 rupiahs (1.2 euro) per day is paid and the average monthly income is two million rupiahs (167 euro), is very high", explains the carrier, who previously worked as a bricklayer on the tourist island of Bali.

There he earned 75,000 rupiahs (6.2 euros) a day, and the work was not so hard, but Anto returned with his family to Banyuwangi, a village nearby, for a reason that is as important in Indonesia as sulphur: "I married a girl from Bali, where they are Hindus, and I brought her to Java to convert her to Islam."
Anto has asthma, he has difficulty breathing, he is coughing a lot and his eyes are irritated because of the toxic gases.
