The 27-year-old Anto has been risking his life for three years at the Ijen volcano, where the sulfur has already left its mark on his face, even though he covers his face with a mask and special glasses.
Anto has asthma, he has difficulty breathing, he is coughing a lot and his eyes are irritated because of the toxic gases from the volcano.
This is the price he has to pay to achieve his dream.
"I will be working here for two more years because I want to open a shop or learn Spanish or French," he promises in a more than adequate English.
This young man, who is charming, intelligent, but has been punished by life, could work as a tourist guide, waiter or hotel receptionist, but instead he is doing the work of a porter.
He shares a filthy wooden hut with other carriers and gets up at two in the morning because the sulphur also emanates at night, where its characteristic yellow colour glows blue in the darkness.
The shadows challenging, he climbs into the crater in the light of a small headlamp he bought with his own money.
About 400 carriers load their baskets with sulphur on their shoulders.

Despite its large profits, the mining company has not mechanized the sulphur extraction to save costs, and does not provide any equipment to the carriers who work on their own account and are paid by weight.

You also do not get a share of the 30,000 rupee (2.5 euro) surcharge per camera, which the guards of this nature park together with the entrance fee of 15,000 rupee (1.2 euro) demand from tourists who come to photograph the volcano and the human pack animals.
"This work is for the animals and not for the people" protests Madrusin, a sturdy, 42-year-old carrier who has been working for three decades since leaving school at Kawah Ijen.
He is able to carry up to 110 kg and assures that he will continue "as long as it is possible" because he needs the money to educate his three children aged between 10 and 18 years.
I will not retire, I will die here because the volcano has been my whole life.

Even if the sulfur burns the throat and the eyes itch, if the wind suddenly turns and the miners are trapped in the thick pillars that rise from the crater, the men are so tough that no one complains about serious illnesses ... of course except for the usual problems of breathing, arthritis, pain in the knees and blisters on the shoulders that have been deformed by the weight of the baskets.
With the basket on his back, Unainik, at 53 years old, can only carry 50 kg.
Every day he and his companions break 15 tons of sulfur from the volcano, which is transported by three trucks through a goat path between the bushes to the camp in Tamansari 18 kilometers away.
"I will not retire, I will die here because the volcano has been my whole life" explains Unainik, opening his mouth wide, with some teeth missing.
Of his five children, the oldest, at 30 years old, also works as a carrier of sulfur.
Time passes, but poverty holds generations in one of the world’s most difficult jobs: carrying human burdens on the Kawah Ijen.
Singapore needs babies to save the economy
Singaporeans blame their lack of children on career, stress and the cost of housing and child-rearing.
"Singapore's population must grow."
I am a patriotic husband, you are my patriotic wife: let us fulfil our civic duty and create life!
It is hard to believe that the verses are part of an ad for mint candies, but nevertheless - or perhaps because of that - they became a viral video on YouTube earlier this year in Singapore.
The lines are part of a rapper's song that mocks local sayings such as "pushing will put a 'bao' (loaf) in the oven to make fun of the low birth rate in Singapore.
The advertising agency BBH, which produced the video, hopes that the ad will bring attention to the problem in a lighthearted way.
Its creative director Douglas Hamilton said he wanted to use the power of music to get people to fulfill their "national duty."
This is something only for the Internet, so we had to make it funny and witty.
This is the biggest problem in this country.
In reproduction we are the worst in the world, so we noticed that it was a subject that we had to take care of.
We knew that the government had tried many things, such as marketing perfume with pheromones or organising speed-dating events.
It is possible that many of these ideas were creative, but they did not necessarily lead to success.
Therefore, we thought: why not make something as creative as possible to address this problem, such as composing a rap?
1.2 children
The government of Singapore is not taking this lightly.
Each year it spends $1,300 on political measures to encourage citizens to have more children.
A package of the government for couples and parents grants up to $15,000 per child, extends maternity leave and distributes tax benefits.
But all of this has been little success so far.
Singapore is a wealthy, high-tech city-state in Southeast Asia, known for its conservative rulers and strict social controls.
According to its national population agency, the fertility rate is currently 1.2 children per woman.
The last time that this rate was over 2 - what is also known as the replacement rate - was in 1976.
So why are Singaporeans having fewer children?
Tan Wei Ming, director of family policy at the National Population and Immigration Board, says that this is due to "better education" and "greater career opportunities".
"This has enabled people to have much more choice in terms of life goals and priorities other than just getting married and having a family," she explains.

These changes in social conditions have contributed to the increase in the number of single people and to the postponement of marriage and childbirth, which has resulted in a decline in Singapore's fertility rate.
Meanwhile, a policy of immigration aimed at reducing the population by attracting large numbers of immigrants has led to resentment among local people.

In Singapore there are websites where the barely concealed xenophobia against many new immigrants is flourishing, especially against the Chinese, who are criticised for keeping wages low and not integrating.
The rise of immigration is also seen as one of the reasons why the ruling party in Singapore suffered its worst electoral result since independence last year.
Since the elections, an attempt has been made to correct the problem of higher contributions and taxes for foreign workers.
Unexpected consequences
While the declining birth rate has the well-known effects on a nation’s economic growth, tax revenues, health care costs, and immigration policy, Singapore’s example shows unexpected consequences.
The government is trying to ensure that not as many small apartments are built.
It has already had an impact on the housing market.
The City Development Authority has begun to control the number of small apartments known as "shoe boxes" that are allowed to be built in certain areas of the city.
These apartments have a living area of 46 square meters and have been a great success.
However, there is concern that they may encourage the lifestyle of the single person, and that they may discourage builders from building large housing for families.
But Lim Yew Soon, managing director of EL Developers, says that his "shoe boxes" are selling much faster than larger units.
They are so popular, and units are selling out days and even weeks before the larger units.
This makes them much better for our cash flow.
He does, however, acknowledge that the new standards will give developers clearer guidance than was previously available, when they wanted to build too many small units within a project.
Too much stress
Singapore is a city-state.
Even if these new rules could pave the way to an increase in the national birth rate, the talks with Singaporeans working in the financial district suggest that they will have little impact.
"People are stressed, housing and education are expensive, so it is being put off by many" says a young manager.
The children can get others.
"For me it is important to have my own money and time" says another, twenty-year-old man.
Men and women are leading their careers, stress and the cost of property and education as reasons why they cannot have children.
That is why Singapore has the last word when it comes to having children - no matter how much the government may want to do.
The offline private is online private
Privacy
According to the dictionary, it is the property of being private or "that part of private life where one has the right to protection from any interference".
What is private for someone under 16?
How is this definition applied to his everyday life and social networks?
Does he understand the dangers he is exposing himself to by posting online situations he would not share in real life?
El Periódico interviewed five teenagers aged between 10 and 15 years old who are often online.
In four of the cases they linked the term to "something very personal" on a personal level and "to the password and the user" when they applied it to the social networks.

"My deepest secrets I would not post in a post" says the 10-year-old Jorge trying to explain the meaning of "private" in websites like Facebook, Twitter, Hotmail and Windows Live Messenger where he has accounts for two years.
"These are very confidential secrets, my mother may know them, but not the whole world," he confirms.
On FB I upload nice pictures or pictures of games.
I also spend time with friends.
"I will not share a photo that is not mine or someone who is doing the dumb thing" he says.
The boy is aware that it is wrong to publish obscene photos, of naked people, of crimes, or to write insulting or violent comments.
Jorge claims to know 35 friends on Facebook and nine followers on Twitter.
Most are relatives.
This includes the mother, who has the password to one of the accounts.
I signed up to Twitter to express myself and to write interesting tweets.
"I do not know if anyone will answer me, I just upload them" he adds.
"Social networks are fun, I can quickly talk to relatives far away or with friends" he says.
He replies that he would never accept an invitation from an unknown person.
Even if someone were to introduce him to a stranger, he would ignore it.
The case of 14-year-old José is different.
The teenager has user accounts in Hotmail, Facebook, My Space and Ask. In Ask he admits he does not know 20 of the people he added to his friend list.
"It does not frighten me because we have something in common, for example music," he says.
According to the Young man, no one has given him any hints or asked for his address or phone number.
"If someone harasses me or asks me to remove them from my account, I simply remove them from my account" he admits.
José contacted Ask after reading a recommendation on Twitter.
The young people are not unfamiliar with experiences that we now know as cyberbullying.
A friend of mine was held hostage in a social network.
They threatened him and demanded money.
"He never knew who it was," he says.
According to José, the victim did not close the account.
"He did it privately."
Then he explains a number of steps to securely configure a user account.
Unlike Jorge, this boy would upload photos of friends in awkward or embarrassing situations.
Yes, I would do that if I dislike him or if I want to get even with him.
"But I know that this is cyberbullying" he explains.
Key issues

Marielos Porras, English teacher with a degree in Education and Learning, says that in order to orient children and young people, it is necessary to understand that the purpose of social networks is to inform.
"The Internet was created as a medium for the search for information; but with the appearance of these pages the rules have changed," she says.

Porras explains that the academic Marc Prensky, holder of a Master's degree in Education at Yale University and author of the book "Digital Natives and Immigrants" created these terms to explain the phenomenon.
Digital Natives are the children and young people who have grown up with this technology.
"We are the digital immigrants who are teaching them where we ourselves are still learning" he says.

He explains that it is a complex issue, "because we are asking them to have a defined criterion about what is to be published, broadcast or said, and this at an age where they are not mature enough to make that choice."
"They should also be selective when it comes to being popular, having thousands of friends without thinking about the consequences," he adds.
According to the expert, the most effective way to teach children and young people what privacy is to ask them questions that make them think.
"To tell them not to do it doesn't work," he says.
Porras then mentions some of the things you would not tell a stranger. Why do you do it on the Internet?
Or: Would you like it if someone posted a picture of you, like the one you posted of a friend?
Do you know what the others are saying about you?
Have you asked the other people's permission before you have taken pictures of their parties?
And one more question: must everyone know what you are doing at any given moment?
Another point is to make them understand that they must act online as they do offline.
They are the same rules.
"Someone outside the Internet is acting with respect, decency and other principles, and the same must be true for social networks," he says.
Monitoring
Estuardo Guardia, university professor, primary school teacher and educational consultant, comments that it is essential that parents carefully read the guidelines of the social networks.
If they understand all the sections, they will have a solid foundation to talk to their children about the importance of opening a user account on the Internet.
"For example, age, or what you can share or publish" he explains.
According to the Guardia, children must be reminded of the lesson "Do not talk to strangers"
The Summit of the Union of South American Nations without the publication of the Lima Declaration

The sixth Summit of the Presidents of the Union of South American Nations (Unasur) ended today in Peru without the publication of the Lima Declaration, which had been announced and was supposed to be signed by the seven leaders present.

Efe repeatedly tried to gain access to the signed document at the VI Ordinary Session of the Heads of State and Government of the Unasur. Sources in the State and President's Office initially said that they would hand it over after the closing, but later said that it would be published at some point on the Peruvian Government's website.
As to the text, they said that the content was explained by the President of Peru, Ollanta Humala, in brief statements to the press.
Access to information about the summit was restricted at every stage.
During the day, the press room was only shown the picture of the President's meeting without sound, with the message "private meeting, limited audio".
The few information that circulated among the journalists were obtained from the press officers of some of the countries that were present at the meeting, but not from the Peruvian press officer.

The only document circulated during the day was the list of participating presidents, which caused unease among the hundreds of journalists from various national and international media who demanded more information.
Then, the Peruvian Presidency sent an e-mail to the media with the "closing statement" of the summit, but it was the statement of President Humala and not the official document of the summit.

Last October, Peru was the host of the III Summit of South America - Arab States (ASPA), and on that occasion, despite the press's insistence, the so-called Lima Declaration, which had been announced beforehand, was not published.
On the official ASPA website you can see that the document was published last Tuesday.
At both international meetings, Peruvian authorities stressed that the information systems for journalists were in place, but they were restricting access to information to a high degree.
The summit also ended with a joint commitment by Chile and Peru to accept a ruling by the Hague-based International Court of Justice that upholds a border dispute between the two countries.

The presidents of Peru, Ollanta Humala, and Chile, Sebastián Piñera, met during the regional meeting and confirmed that they would accept the decision of the IGH, which begins on Monday in The Hague, to hear the pleadings of both parties in the process that Lima initiated against Santiago.
"We will follow and carry out the judgment that we are now presenting to this international court," said Humala, speaking with his Chilean counterpart.

"Chile is, is and will continue to be a country that respects international law, seeks peaceful solutions to disputes, makes agreements and submits to the international courts," adds Piñera, who shook hands with Humala before the flags of both countries.

The confirmation of both Presidents that they would be subject to the IGH came after Colombia had filed a lawsuit against the Bogota Agreement, which it considered a grave mistake, in which it agreed to be subject to the rulings of this International Court of Justice.
The summit was attended by the presidents of Brazil, Dilma Rousseff, Venezuela, Hugo Chávez, Bolivia, Evo Morales, and Argentina, Cristina Kirchner.
Paraguay, which was suspended from the Unasur in 2011 after the suspension of its president Fernando Lugo, did not participate in the meeting.
The host President Ollanta Humala opened the talks in the morning and closed the summit shortly after lunchtime in Lima.

The President read the final document, in which it was stated that 16 decisions were taken and the action lines for 31 projects were established between the South American countries for an investment of a total of $17 billion.

Among the decisions taken, he said that the countries of the Unasur "will take significant steps towards the goal of a South American citizenship, to which we will extend the decisions on residence rights."

He said that measures were being advanced to "improve cooperation in the fight against insecurity in the cities and against organized crime, as well as measures to improve access to medicines and the Internet at low prices in all areas of South America and to act together and efficiently in the event of natural disasters".

The crisis in Europe must not be an excuse for economic consolidation (in Latin America) to take on a triumphant tone, but should be used to expand our production capacity and show our peoples a better future, he added.

"We have decided to give priority to a number of 31 emblematic projects that will improve the spatial connections in South America and especially in rural and border areas...and thus unite our countries and open up new forms of economic activity", said the Peruvian President in a read statement.

Among these projects would be five Peruvian, which would be on the axis of its territory from the coast to Brazil, and of which two would be to improve the connection with Ecuador, although he did not give any further details.
The final document also referred to the political situation in Paraguay.
"We hope that the electoral process in this country will serve to re-establish it in the Union of South American Nations, of which it is currently excluded.
The need for Latin America to continue to be an integrated region for prosperity and peace and with good neighborly relations was another aspect that was emphasized at the summit.

In that sense, President of Colombia Juan Manuel Santos said before the start of the regional meeting that he expected to meet on Saturday in Mexico with his counterpart from Nicaragua, Daniel Ortega, to respect the maritime conflict after a ruling by the IGH that was challenged by Bogota.
"I may meet President Daniel Ortega tomorrow (Saturday)," said Santos.
"We will all look at all these ways - they are not exclusive, and the agreement with Nicaragua makes it necessary to have talks with Nicaragua," he stressed.
"I hope to be able to tell President Ortega that we will treat this matter as civilly and respectfully as possible," Santos added.
Santos and Ortega are scheduled to meet on Saturday in Mexico, where they intend to be present at the inauguration of the new president of that country, Enrique Peña Nieto.
As part of the summit, the defence ministers of the group also met in advance to adopt the action plan for 2013, which aims to strengthen dialogue and consensus on defence in the region.
Argentina, Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, Uruguay, Venezuela, Chile, Guyana, Suriname and Paraguay are members of UNASUR, although the latter is currently excluded.
Peru has the presidency of the regional bloc for a period.
"South America must learn to integrate its citizens," says Rafael Correa
President of Ecuador, Rafael Correa, confirmed today that the creation of a common citizenship is a goal, saying that "South America can actually learn something from Europe."

Correa, who attended the 6th Summit of the Presidents of the Union of South American Nations (Unasur) held in Lima, said to Peruvian state television that Europeans "killed each other in the Second World War and in other conflicts" and "today are practically one country."
In this sense, he defended the project of creating a South American citizenship that the member states of Unasur are promoting.

"Free movement of citizens and workers must be achieved in all South American countries, as is the case in the Andean Community; however, there are reactionary sectors that seek to return to the past", he warned.

The President of Ecuador also endorsed the re-launching of the Organization of American States (OAS) with the aim of reducing the influence of the Anglo-Saxon countries and of taking into account those that have signed the San José agreement on human rights.
The ones who teach never commit to anything, and in return we always sign everything with the South Americans.

"It is incomprehensible that the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights is based in Washington and is funded by the United States," he said, referring to the political asylum that Ecuador has granted to the founder of WikiLeaks, Julian Assange.
Correa assured that he was not sorry for having made that decision because he had not betrayed his principles, but had fulfilled his "deep democratic values and respect for human rights".
He added that there had been "well-founded suspicions that Assange would be extradited to a third country and his trial would not be fair."

He also criticized Swedish justice, which he said had demanded that he be subjected to interrogation on its territory for an alleged sexual offense, while "Swedish law allows this to be done by video-conference, which could have been done through the Ecuadorian embassy in London."
Correa said that there was a risk that Assange’s health and mental state would be affected.
"Since he has been in our embassy, I have not spoken to him, but the ambassador has informed me that he has a slight problem with his lungs, but nothing serious," said the Ecuadorian president.
However, there is a risk that he will suffer physical and mental harm because he is confined in a small space and cannot exercise in the open air.
"This would affect the health of every person," he added.

Correa claimed that the solution to the asylum that Assange has been granted since June in the Ecuadorian embassy in London was the granting of a passport, by which he could travel to Ecuador, and that this was in the hands of the UK, Sweden and the legal authorities of Europe. He stressed that there had been talks with London to find a solution for the imprisoned founder of WikiLeaks.
We are not trading in human rights, we are not using that word for this case, but there have been constant discussions.

"The solution to this problem is in the hands of Britain, Sweden and the European legal authorities , because Assange's lawyer, Baltazar Garzón, is conducting a series of proceedings in various European jurisdictions , " he said.
And "if Britain tomorrow grants this license, I think it is done."
And if Sweden were to interrogate Mr Assange at the Ecuadorian embassy in London or via Skype, as Swedish law allows and has been done in other cases, the problem would be solved.
Correa used the occasion to reaffirm his commitment to freedom of the press and said that what he does not tolerate "is mediocrity, evil intent and the lie that subverts free expression."
"The greatest enemies of press freedom are not the evil and perverse politicians, but bad journalists who seek profit and blackmail," he said.

In this sense, he congratulated himself that Ecuador is no longer "controlled by journalists and also by bankers or by hegemonic and bourgeois countries," and he anticipated that, in the event of a re-election, he will "deepen the revolution to continue on the path in the right direction."

Correa also supported the decision to maintain the veto against Paraguay in the Unasur at least until its next elections, arguing that the organism "must remain firm and not allow any opportunism and any coup d'état disguised as legal" because "the legitimacy of democracy in Paraguay has been destroyed."

The Ecuadorian president also considers the desire of his Colombian counterpart, Juan Manuel Santos, to negotiate maritime borders with Nicaragua now and after the ruling of the International Court of Justice that favored Nicaragua's maritime sovereignty, to be "absolutely legitimate."
This judgment is not being implemented at present.
It is a problem between a South American country and a Central American country.
Conflicts are inevitable, but they must be overcome in the quest for a common path.
They must be treated comprehensively so that we can overcome them and look forward.

He also trusted that the dispute over maritime borders between Peru and Chile would be settled by the same court, and he said that "it is right for Latin America to call on international bodies when both countries agree to accept the decision, even if it is very harsh."

Regarding the possibility that he will run for a third consecutive term as president of Ecuador, he said that he sees this possibility "with great optimism and joy, although it is sometimes very difficult."
Correa assured that, if he lost the elections in February 2013, he would withdraw from the political life.
Power has never been of interest to me personally, but under such unfair conditions as exist in Ecuador, this socio-economic poverty can only be corrected by political power.
"My political movement had the belief that I was the one who guaranteed this possible victory, so I must fulfill this responsibility," he said.
If I were to win, it would be my last term as President, after which I would retire from public life.
This is also true when we lose.
"It is decided," he said.
Correa also referred to the treatment of President Hugo Chávez’s health problems in Cuba.

I have just spoken to the Vice-President of Venezuela, Nicolás Maduro. He has told me that he has travelled there for a routine treatment, and that he is expected to be able to travel back to Cuba after the campaign.
"In no way does it represent a relapse in President Chávez's health condition," he commented.

The Ecuadorian President participated today in Lima at the 6th Summit of the Heads of State and Government of the Union of South American Nations (UNASUR), which concluded with the call for greater regional integration to ensure sustainable progress, equality and security.
The cause of death from AIDS today is a late diagnosis
Fabrizio was 21 when he was told the results of his test: he was HIV-positive.
"It was like a bomb had gone off," he says of the moment he received the diagnosis, which the doctor tried to 'soften' without any apparent success.
He hid it from his family.
He decided to take care of his illness himself and began to inform himself; and he did so with such commitment that he was celebrating his 43rd birthday.
He is undoubtedly one of the oldest patients in the HIV unit of the Hospital Civil de Guadalajara (HCG), where he arrived after several battles in 1994.

Fabrizio has been living with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) for 22 years, which was difficult to imagine in the early 1990s, when there were many doubts, few treatment options and more stigma.
At that time, even the director of a hospital of the IMSS avoided saying goodbye, "because it led to a dead end."
At that time, AIDS was synonymous with death.
Today it is possible to survive this syndrome with quality of life.

However, many people are still coming into the hospital who do not know they have the disease and who have already been infected and exhausted their immune system, and who are victims of opportunistic infections.

31 years after the appearance of AIDS in the world, i. e. after the appearance of the first reported cases, "the great success today is that the survival of a patient who takes the treatment on time and the survival of the general population are exactly the same", said the head of the HIV unit of the HCG, Jaime Andrade Villanueva, saying that this information was supported in April of this year by a respected scientific publication.

The specialist in infectious diseases and HIV/AIDS, Dr. Andrade Villanueva, commented that scientists have been concluding since 2008 that AIDS is not a death sentence, but that the years of survival and quality of life depend on the degree of impairment of the immune system of the person at the start of treatment, and that those with greater chances are those who are not drug addicts: up to 30 years at a count of 200 CD4 and 50 years at a count of 500 CD4.
Simply put, the above statements mean that, if someone is diagnosed HIV-positive at age 25, he or she can live "problem-free for 75 years as long as he or she is under control," said the expert.
To properly assess this progress, it must be remembered that the average life expectancy of Mexicans today is 76 years.

Even though mortality has decreased significantly in recent years (in Mexico, the number of people dying from AIDS has decreased from 6,678 cases in 2007 to 4,862 in 2011 (UNAIDS Annual Report), it is still true that 60% of the patients registered in the national database have died since the disease was first identified.
In Jalisco alone, 255 people died in 2011, and by May of this year, there have been 187 deaths; however, it is assured that universal access to antiretroviral drugs has been in place since 2005.
- Why are people still dying from it?
- In my opinion, the problem is not access to treatment.
This is my opinion, and so it is in our hospital.

At least in the last 12 years we have not had any problems with medicines. The problem is that people come in very late stages of the disease because they do not know their infection status, i. e. in very late stages of the disease.

It makes a powerful statement: "Nine out of ten patients come to us with an accompanying infection. To influence global mortality, earlier diagnoses are needed, which means that all people who need them must be offered massive screening tests."

This proposal is supported by the experts and officials of the Consejo Estatal de Prevención del Sida en Jalisco (Coesida) (State Council for AIDS Prevention in Jalisco) and also by patients like Fabrizio, who had his test done at a private laboratory, for the simple reason that a friend of his had already been in the AIDS stage, even having Kaposi's sarcoma (a cancer-like tumor), which is one of the usual complications.
Everything is different when you know you have AIDS.
Some think they will die, and want nothing to do with it.
"If I have to die, I would rather explode three times," is what they say in my case.
The amendment was to improve, I eat well, I do sports and I take the drugs.
Today his parents only know that he had cancer.
I live a normal life, like everyone else.

"I work, I do a lot, I have an active but responsible sex life, I take care of my health and that of the other person," says Fabrizio, who agreed to share his intimate details with MILENIO JALISCO to encourage those who today are afraid of AIDS.
You should take the test if you are at risk. The earlier you know if you are HIV-positive, the better, and if you already know the diagnosis, you should learn how to live responsibly like all people.
His message is a summary of the fight against AIDS in 2012.
Condoms behind the counter
There are huge gaps between the health programmes and the simple citizen, explains Ricardo Salazar, a journalist who has taken up the cause of HIV.
And the most important thing is prevention.

At the designated places "the distribution of condoms has actually increased; before they were given out individually, now they give us packages of one hundred, which is already good, but there are still people who do not have access to a condom", he said.
The risk group for new infections includes young people.
"Why do you need it?" is a common taunt from social workers, school counselors, pharmacists, and health-care workers who want to keep young people from using it, the correspondent said.
He proposed that this inefficient distribution be reoriented; condoms should not only be behind the counter, but in dispensing devices in public toilets in facilities frequented by young people.
It should not promote promiscuity.
It should not be paid for beer and motel, as Governor Emilio González replied to the question of whether he would distribute condoms under his administration.
"Sexuality is not what it used to be; the best thing is to bring condoms closer to those who already have sex," he said.
Key data from Jalisco
There are 13,435 cumulative cases (12,158 AIDS and 1,317 HIV).
The country is ranked fourth in the number of new and cumulative cases of AIDS, and 13th in the number of cases of HIV.
92% of infections occur through sexual contact, 6% through blood and 2% perinatally.
It is estimated that 50,000 people are living with HIV because for every registered case there are 4 or 5 people who do not know.

After the United States Court of Appeals has upheld a judgment that does not recognize the restructuring of the group's debt that was achieved through a Mexican commercial bankruptcy, a pernicious precedent is being created for any national company with subsidiaries in the neighboring country that has payment problems.
Thus, one could say that the procedures for the survival of the companies that the Mexican laws allow are in conflict with international agreements in the land of the stars and stripes.

In practice, the recognition of the 15 June judgment by Judge Harlin Hale of the Court in Bancarrotas for the Northern District of Texas means that Mexican companies are left helpless to face the confiscation of their property across the river.
However, the decision opens the door for the largest glass manufacturer in Mexico to call the Supreme Court of the United States to challenge three inconsistencies.

While the judge of the case points out that creditors must be subject to the United States bankruptcy law, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans initially says that the main case is the commercial bankruptcy in Mexico.
The first point would be that international cooperation in procedures for the insolvency of companies with a cross-border profile is not known.
Indeed, the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods was created for this purpose, with the American Law Institute acting as a mediator.

Second, the judgment determines that without the votes of the companies after recognition of the liabilities in the bankruptcy estate, which the subsidiaries of Vitro had with their parent company, the required majority for the restructuring of the liabilities would not have been reached.
However, this possibility is recognized by Mexican law.
In fact, this is not the first time that this scheme has been approved.

There are a half-dozen examples, including Agremex and Comercial Mexicana, whose debts have been confirmed by the Instituto Federal de Concursos Mercantiles (Federal Institute of Commercial Insolvencies).

It is also true that after deducting the votes of the branches, the creditors of Vitro, the creditors who sued Vitro in the courts of the United States, i. e. the vultures funds such as Aurelios Capital, Aurelios Convergencia, Elliot Internacional and Liverpool Limited, would not have reached a majority.
The vote would have been 45% against 37%.
This is not taken into account by the Court of Appeal.
On the other hand, Vitro is to blame for its difficult situation since 2008 in the context of the great economic crisis in the United States, which hit the country.

For this reason, the González Sada family has lodged an appeal before the same court of appeal, so that the vote in the plenary session takes place, i. e. by all the judges, because only three of them voted.
If that is not granted, the Cerciorare appeal will be lodged, which calls for a review of the procedure by a higher instance, in this case by the Supreme Court of the United States.

The serious thing about this case is that the Court ignored a document sent to it by the Mexican Government under the figure of amicus curiae, in which the procedure carried out by Vitro under the law on commercial conciliation is described, and in which it is stated that it was strictly following the agreements signed between the two countries to comply with Chapter 15 of the United States Bankruptcy Law.

It is also pointed out that the country has committed itself to the principles of the United Nations Commission on International Trade, i. e. to the rules on cross-border insolvency, which guarantee equality between debtors and creditors.
Two-handed billiards: a shot for Vitro and for the country.

Héctor "Hetin" Reyes: "Basketball was my life"
The world traveler of basketball, Héctor "Hetin" Reyes, has been connected to the sport for more than 60 years and has traveled the world.
Few in Puerto Rico have such a vast collection of the history of the sport in the island as Héctor "Hetin" Reyes.

Before he was paralyzed by a stroke in 2008, Rex had been part of this sport for 6 years, whether as a player in lower classes, a player in the first national league, a delegate and director in the BSN with the Vaqueros de Bayamón or president of the basketball federation.

"I have worn many hats in basketball, even several at the same time, when I was president of the BSN, general manager of the national team and president of the federation in the 90's," Reyes recalled during a visit to Primera Hora at his home in Bayamón, where he lives with Isabel, his faithful wife for more than 50 years.
"Basketball was my life."
Reyes is not exaggerating.
The walls of his house are almost all decorated with photos and memories of his long career and they testify to it.
Bayamón in the heart
The most emotional memories are those of his time with the Vaqueros from the mid-1950s as a player until 1982 when he celebrated his 15th anniversary as a club manager or director.
"Those were my best years, the ones I enjoyed the most because I was part of eight championships of the Vaqueros since 1967 whether as manager, co-manager or coach.
It was a very fulfilling period, including five consecutive championships from 1971 to 1975.
And then I said goodbye with a championship in 1981, the year of the debut of Jerome Mincy with BSN.
From then on, "Cuco" Ortiz, who was a very good administrator, took over the reins of the company,
I remember Gene Bartow, who was a trainer here and was employed at the University of Alabama (Birmingham), saying: "I have a very strong and 2 m tall player.
Would you like it?
And that was the beginning of Mincy, one of the best players Puerto Rico ever had.
Bartow then recommended the specialist in free throws, Raymond Gausse, who became a citizen and was one of our best shooters.
I remember him saying that if Mincy had made a championship possible for Bayamon, Gausse would make another possible.
The championship of the Vaqueros with Gausse was granted to him, but already at a distance, because he was already at the top of the association in 1988.
At that time, he preferred to enjoy his executions and those of Mincy in the national team.
I remember when we won our first match against the USA at the pre-Olympic tournament in Mexico.
Then came the 1990 World Championship, where we finished fourth, which should have been bronze, if not for that Canadian referee who made us repeat the last move for the second time, said Reyes.
Was was the World Cup group of 1990 the best national team you have ever seen?
She is one of the best, as well as one of the best in the world, having won the gold medal in the 2004 Olympic Games against the Dream Team.
My favorite team was the 1991 Pan American Games team in Cuba, where we won gold and gave the USA a fight, as they did to us in the World Championships when they won bronze.

In that team were not only Mincy, Gausse, Ramon Rivas, Fico López and "Piculín" (Ortiz) again, but also the young players (Javier) "Toñito" Colón and James Carter, the brothers León (Francisco and Edgar) and Mario "Quijote" Morales, who was unable to play in 1990 due to a knee injury.
A team that was perhaps not the best in terms of personalities, but that won a gold medal and brought us great joy, was that of the pre-Olympic tournament in Neuquén, Argentina, in 1995.

With players like "Canito" Nieves, Pablo Alicea and the young Rolando Hourruitiner as a replacement for the suspended players due to the events at the Pan American Games in Mar del Plata, we won the gold medal against all odds.
Who was the best Puerto Rican player?
It was without doubt Piculín Ortiz.
His numbers on the international circuit are impressive.
No one in Puerto Rico has dominated at this level like Piculín.
And this, without taking into account his career in the different leagues in which he has played.
Who was the best coach in Puerto Rico?
This is a difficult question.
We had a number of good trainers like Julio Toro, Flor Meléndez, Carlos Morales, Raymond Dalmau, Armandito Torres.
I like Leo Arill's work.
What do you think is the best thing you have achieved in the association?
I was part of the most successful era of the national team from 1988 to 1995, which included up to 17 teams in a season at the beginning of the 90's.
What else is there for you to do?
There are things I would have introduced, such as the regionalisation of the lower categories.
That the boys in Ponce, for example, only play in their area and only meet teams from other parts of the island in the national playoffs.
Today, children make unnecessary journeys and play.
At least I see the result of the compulsory training and courses for trainers, table officials and referees.
I am proud of this.
What are you doing today?
I enjoy listening to music, watching videos of music from my time on YouTube, enjoying my grandchildren and sometimes going to a basketball game.
And of course I enjoy the company of my wife Isabel, who has always been by my side.

Larry Hagman, whose role as oil tycoon J.R. Ewing in the television series "Dallas" became a symbol of the greed of the 1980s, has died.

Republican leaders justified their policy by the need to combat electoral fraud.

Indeed, Republican lawyers identified only 300 cases of electoral fraud in the United States in a decade.
One thing is certain: these new provisions will have a negative impact on voter turn-out.
In this sense, the measures will partially undermine the American democratic system.
Unlike in Canada, the American States are responsible for the organisation of federal elections in the United States.
It is in this spirit that a majority of American governments have passed new laws since 2009 making the registration or voting process more difficult.
This phenomenon gained momentum following the November 2010 elections, which saw 675 new Republican representatives added in 26 States.
As a result, 180 bills restricting the exercise of the right to vote in 41 States were introduced in 2011 alone.
The new election laws require voters to show a photo ID card and proof of US citizenship.
Furthermore, these laws also reduce early voting periods, invalidate the right to register as a voter on election day and withdraw the right to vote of citizens with a criminal record.
Before the 2006 elections, no US State required voters to show a photo ID card.
Indiana was the first State to impose such a requirement.
In 2008, the Supreme Court of the United States upheld the constitutionality of the Indiana law.
The Republican authorities were quick to extend this practice to other States.
Over the past two years, they sponsored bills in 34 States to force voters to show a photo ID card.
It is important to note that, unlike Quebec, American citizens do not have a universal ID card such as the health insurance card.
In fact, 11% of American citizens, i.e. 21 million people of voting age, do not possess a photo ID card issued by a government agency of their State.
In addition, five million new voters in 2012 do not have such identification.
And it often costs over a hundred dollars to obtain the required identity card.
The new restrictions disproportionately affect young people, minorities and people with low incomes.
In fact, 25% of African Americans, 15% of those earning less than $35,000; 18% of citizens over 65 and 20% of voters 18 to 29 years old do not have the required photo ID card.
And that's not all.
Students, voters considered to be voting more for Democratic candidates, are not allowed in several States to use the photo ID card issued by their institution.
On the other hand, these same States allow fishing or hunting club members, who vote more Republican, to use the cards issued by these clubs when they vote.
Prior to 2004, no State required proof of citizenship to vote.
Arizona was the first to introduce such a requirement.
Since 2011, a dozen States have adopted laws requiring voters to prove they are American citizens.
These measures are clearly intended to limit the Hispanic vote.
However, it appears that two out of three Hispanic voters favour the Democratic party.
What is more, in 2011 Republican legislators sponsored laws abolishing the registration of voters on election day in eight States.
In addition, they limited the right of individuals and groups to provide assistance to voters wishing to register.
These restrictions are not without consequence.
For example, during the 2004 general election, voter registration campaigns contributed to registering around 10 million citizens.
However, the measures adopted since 2009 have led to a 17% drop in the registration rate of new voters in 2010 compared to 2006.
In addition, Republican legislators have enacted laws in five other States aimed at reducing the early voting period.
For example, during the 2008 general election in Florida, 33% of early voters were African-Americans, who accounted however for only 13% of voters in the State.
The same applied to Hispanics.

On the other hand, 76% of voters were white but these represented only 46% of early voters.
Of course, Democratic legislators and their supporters vigorously opposed the adoption of laws restricting voter registration.
Several bills were blocked by vetoes of Democratic governors.
The United States Attorney General intervened to suspend the most controversial laws.
They were able to partially limit the damage.

However, the new rules put in place will undoubtedly make it more difficult to exercise the right to vote in 2012.
Democratic critics denounce the partisan character of the laws that have been passed and they see a clear objective of influencing the 2012 results in key States.
A 2011 Brennan Centre report shows that the States that have adopted these laws represent 171 of the 270 votes needed in the electoral college to win the Presidency.
It is too early to say with certainty that these legislative changes in the electoral system will have significant impacts on the outcome of the 2012 presidential elections.

In this sense, the measures will partially undermine the American democratic system.
Prostate cancer screening: take the test or not?
Indeed, the PSA test sometimes shows erroneous results with false negative or even false positive results, which involve unnecessary medical interventions.
Enough to make already reluctant men hesitate to take screening tests.
Take the test or not?
We asked two specialists for their opinion.
In studies conducted in the United States, there was a lot of contamination between control groups, so it is difficult to interpret the data and make firm recommendations.
Another study, this time a European one, concluded that there was a difference in mortality between patients who were screened and those who were not.
This study also showed, with a follow-up after 12 years, that it is between 30 and 40% more likely for metastases to occur in the absence of screening.
I therefore recommend the test from age 50, or 40 if you have a direct relative who previously had prostate cancer.
African-American men are also more at risk.
The key is to make the right decision once cancer has been detected.
There are aggressive cancers and others that are indolent.

The patient really needs to be made to understand the degree of risk of his cancer, by offering him the options available, not necessarily treating prostate cancers that are not long-term life threatening, and opting instead, in such cases, for active monitoring of the disease.
Today, many men in whom cancer has been detected will not be treated because their cancer is not aggressive and is not life threatening.
Active monitoring will be suggested, and if the disease progresses, they will be offered treatment.
More and more, specific criteria are being determined in order to decide who should or should not be treated.
Therefore I recommend taking the test.
But the important thing is to have a discussion with your doctor to determine whether or not to take it.
In collaboration with the Société internationale d'urologie [SIU], Movember has created a tool that makes it possible to evaluate the pros and cons of the PSA test.
You can download the document (in English for the time being, a [French] translation will be available shortly) at this address: http://ca.movember.com/fr/mens-health/prostate-cancer-screening
Preventing the disease
Unfortunately, there is no miracle recipe for preventing cancer.
Despite the progress in research, the adoption of healthy living habits remains the best way to reduce the risk of suffering from it.
It is estimated that if everyone ate well and exercised enough, 30% of cancers could be prevented.
"If no more people smoked, this rate would increase to at least 50%," says André Beaulieu, spokesman for the Canadian Cancer Society.
On the other hand, it is estimated that roughly 10% of cancers are hereditary.
Some are also completely unexplained.
For the Canadian Cancer Society, the fight against tobacco remains a priority, despite the decrease in the number of smokers.
Cigarettes are linked to 85% of lung cancer cases.
It is also a risk factor for a number of others.
This massively damages people's health.
"Even today, there are 1.5 million smokers in Quebec" deplores spokesperson André Beaulieu.
Encouraging data: 10 years after giving up smoking, the risk of dying from cancer drops by half.
Weight
Overweight and obesity are also conducive to the onset of the disease, according to the SCC.
They can increase the risks of cancer of the breast, colon and rectum, oesophagus, pancreas and uterus.
"Research shows that the regular practice of physical activity throughout your life protects against colon cancer" it is also said.
Diet
The organisation also recommends limiting your consumption of red meat.
In large amounts, it increases the risks of developing colo-rectal cancer.
Likewise, so do cured meat products, and these should be avoided.
The conservation of meat by smoking, drying or curing can cause the formation of carcinogens.
"They can damage cells in the body and lead to the development of cancer" it is explained.
Vitamins
In recent years, a number of scientists have studied the links between vitamin supplements and cancer.
For the time being however their research is inconclusive.
Studies on vitamin E are contradictory, according to the SCC.
While one study noted a decrease in the risk of prostate cancer, another noted an increase.

The Higgs boson revealed
The announcement of the probable discovery of the Higgs boson created quite a stir last summer, and with good reason.
Indeed, it is believed that this boson is part of the mechanism responsible for the mass of everything in the Universe, no less.

Also it is the last particle whose existence is predicted by the Standard Model - our best or "less worse" explanation of the nature and behaviour of matter - but which has not yet been observed empirically.
But for physicists, it is still not completely sure that it really is the Higgs.
We know without a shadow of a doubt that it is a new authentic particle, and greatly resembles the Higgs boson predicted by the Standard Model.
In addition, new data unveiled this week at a large physics Congress in Kyoto seem to confirm this, but there are still insufficient data to be perfectly sure.
But let's suppose that it really is the Higgs, since the chances of being mistaken seem slim, and see what it is.
In our world, there is a fatally unavoidable law which states that two things cannot meet at the same place at the same time.
There's no way to break this rule - and don't try too hard, you'll go mad.

However, even though particle physics is a very strange world, it turns out that it also has a law of the same kind: the Pauli exclusion principle, which states that two particles cannot occupy the same space at the same time if they are in the same "quantum state" - this "state" consisting roughly of certain of their characteristics.
Based on this, physicists classify particles into two categories.
In one corner we have good citizens called fermions, who wisely obey the Pauli principle.

While lurking in the other are the bosons, a nasty band of anarchists who respect nothing - at all events, not this principle, which means that they can indeed be found in the same place at the same time.

These bosons are then divided into two groups, according to the Berkeley Labs Particle Adventure site (absolutely extraordinary, by the way): mesons, which we will not discuss here, and "force particles" by which the great forces of nature are propagated and to which the Higgs boson may be somehow related.
These bosons, it must be stressed here, are not all such exotic bugs as you might think.
In fact, if you can read this article, it is thanks to an extraordinarily banal boson: the photon, or the "light particle" which is the "messenger" of the electromagnetic force.
When, in fact, a particle having an electric charge accelerates or changes direction, this "disturbs" the electromagnetic field in this specific place, rather like a pebble thrown in a pond.
This "disturbance" produces an electromagnetic wave (of light, infrared, ultraviolet etc.), and this wave is nothing other than a photon - and thus one of the "force carrier" bosons.
More stable field
The same applies to the Higgs boson, with the difference that it is another field, the Higgs field, which must be "disturbed" for the boson to appear.

Now, this Higgs field is much, much more stable than the electromagnetic field; to excite it, it is necessary to achieve very, very high energy levels, rather like a frozen pond which would need a very large rock to wrinkle the surface.
Which is why a huge particle accelerator like the one at CERN - the Large Hadron Collider is a ring with a 27km circumference! - is needed to achieve such energy levels.
The analogy with the electromagnetic field is again useful for explaining the relationship between the Higgs and mass.
In fact not all particles, or all materials, interact with the electromagnetic field.
Some, such as magnets, do so, but others don't - a piece of paper, for example, will never stick to a fridge.
And likewise, not all particles interact with the Higgs field: those that do so have mass, while the others (such as the photon) do not.
Now, what is it that all this research "can bring"? asks Ms Plamondon.
For science, it serves to check the validity of the Standard Model (SM), and also allows physicians to examine any discrepancies between the observations and predictions of the SM.
A number of people, moreover, fervently hope that some will be found, because the slightest difference could open a door to a "new physics" and plug certain holes in the Model.
This, it must be said, still has huge shortcomings, offering no explanation for gravity (oops!) or dark matter, which forms approximately 80% of the matter in the Universe (re-oops!).
But to date no such discrepancies have been found at CERN.
Repercussions
The repercussions of this research on the daily life of the man in the street are more difficult to predict, but it would be wrong to assume that there won't be any.
Remember: in the very early 60s, the pioneers of the laser at Bell Laboratories did not suspect the revolution that would be triggered by their work.
They had an inkling of the scientific applications, but nothing as to the rest.

In fact, the late Willard Boyle - a physicist who worked at Bell Labs, where the laser was invented in 1960, and who himself developed the first continuous laser (the first were pulsed) in 1962 - told us that initially the laser was rather seen as a "lab gadget."
Just imagine...
And then, applications can also come from all the instrumentation that surrounds research.
For example, the same Willard Boyle developed a small light sensor in 1969, during his work in optics.
This sensor, although this was not at all the original intention, now serves as an "eye" to all digital cameras worldwide, and earned him the Nobel physics prize in 2009.
This does not of course mean that the activities of the LHC will necessarily transform our lives, but it does mean that, actually, you never know...
Palliative care - The best way to die... | Le Devoir
With its Dying with Dignity Commission, Quebec recently discussed the delicate issue of the end of life.
The debate is due to resume shortly as a bill is being prepared.
However, in this vital area, much remains to be done.
Le Devoir attempted to look more closely.
Just a few weeks ago Mr L. lived alone in his Montérégie apartment.
The festering prostate cancer had allowed him a two-year respite.
"They gave me five years to live, I've made it to seven," he says, with mixed emotions, lying in his bed at the Victor-Gadbois palliative care home in Beloeil, where he arrived the previous day.
"But it's still a shock, you can never be prepared for it" he adds.
The disease is doing its work: huge weakness which prevents him going to the toilet alone, and even eating alone.
Sitting in front of an appetising lunch, he consents to being helped to eat, resigned.
Courageous, he even manages to smile, talks to the strangers bustling around him, bringing him his medication, offering him a bath.
The courage of ordinary death.
"What I want most is to be cured of my diarrhoea, it's humiliating" he confided.
A few hours later, the team found a cure for this illness.
"During our lives, we learn that a man pisses standing up," says Pierre Brodeur, psychologist at the Victor-Gadbois home.
Regressing to the stage of a child, for some people, is an unacceptable humiliation.
"It depends on the person's ability" to accept the regression, he says.
Because, in the opinion of a number of people working in palliative care, great moments occur at the very heart of such regression.
Patients at the Victor-Gadbois palliative care home all suffer from cancer.
They have a maximum life expectancy of three months.
At this stage, the team of doctors and nurses surrounding them no longer provides so-called "curative" care.
For Mrs A., 89 years old, the worst fear is to die "conscious and suffocating."
But the disease has made me discover my children.
"I have fine children" she adds.
"I don't wish for anything more in life" she says, before accepting having a mask put on to help her breathe.
She looks forward nevertheless, in the next few days, to a last visit by her son coming from Italy.
At Victor-Gadbois, a group of volunteers provides bodily care and help with feeding.
This is palliative care, given when there is nothing else that can be done.
To make death more comfortable.
In Quebec, there are palliative care beds for 11,700 inhabitants.
This is very few when we know that we will all die one day.
Here, life continues under the best possible conditions, explains Dr Christiane Martel, one of the doctors at the home.
Whether at a physical comfort, emotional or spiritual level.
A person who is dying will accept being helped to drink brandy or Pepsi, whatever is their tipple.
Diabetics no longer need to control their blood sugar.
And death is part of everyday life.
Yesterday evening, a beer was served to Mr X, who died during the night.
This morning, it is his son who will finish the beer at the feet of the deceased.
"We help relatives as much as patients" says Nathalie Savard, Director of Care.
At the Victor-Gadbois home, one day follows another but no two are alike.

Along with a 93-year-old man who is savouring his last meeting with his family, sitting firmly wedged in his pillows while toasts are drunk in his honour, a 36-year-young man is dying tragically, surrounded by his parents, his wife and his two young children, after having tried everything to survive.
"For six months, there have always been three to five beds which are occupied by cancer patients less than 45 years old" says a concerned Dr Christiane Martel.
53% of patients admitted to the Victor-Gadbois home come from their homes, 47% from hospital.
Lack of access to palliative care

It is said that 77% of Canadians simply have no access to palliative care, which is care designed to ease the pain when a patient has reached the terminal stage of life, be it at home, in hospital or in a care home.
And a number of organisations, such as the Victor-Gadbois home and the Palliative Care Society in Greater Montreal, specialise more or less exclusively in care provided to cancer patients.
It is precisely this large gap in Quebec health care which has made a number of palliative care physicians fear the adoption of a law on euthanasia and assisted suicide.
Since October, a manifesto, signed by palliative care luminaries including Dr Balfour Mount and Dr Bernard Lapointe, has been circulating to demonstrate their opposition to such an initiative.
According to Dr Christiane Martel, the Quebec health system is not effective enough to ensure that everyone will be entitled to quality palliative care before it is accepted to proceed to euthanasia.
Recently, she says, I saw a patient spend 14 days in emergency, in great pain, without anything being done to ease her suffering.
I'm afraid that patients ask to die because they don't receive adequate care.
And at the same time, some oncologists work relentlessly on their patients until the last day, despite the worst prognoses.
Hélène Richard's survival hopes were already minimal when she ended her gruelling chemotherapy.
When I announced to my oncologist that I was stopping the treatment, she told me she regretted that I had given up fighting, she said.
However, she had told me I was finished!
No all-powerful care
Dr Martel believes that 90% of patients asking to die thank care-givers for not having acceded to their request after they have been relieved of their pain by a palliative care team.
But it must be said that palliative care is not absolutely all-powerful in the treatment of pain.
According to Elsie Monereau, Palliative Care Director with the Palliative Care Society in Greater Montreal, patients are resistant to treatment against pain in 8% of cases.
At the very end of life, physicians then often resort to palliative sedation, which is equivalent to putting the patient to sleep until the time of death, either sporadically or permanently.
We can no longer pretend not to understand this part of their suffering.
Increasingly, an unrelieved patient will have the option of having such palliative sedation.
Patients who are not relieved always say the same thing: "I want to die."
But this does not necessarily mean "I want you to euthanise me," it means "I want to be relieved."

Then an organiser of the Mayor's party, Martin Dumont, accused Mr Tremblay of having deliberately closed his eyes to a parallel budget feeding his coffers with dirty money.
Following these revelations, Mr Tremblay resigned in early November, plunging Montreal into a major crisis.
Chantal Rouleau was one of the first women in Montreal to raise the alarm.

Mayor of the borough of Rivière-des-Prairies, to the East of the island, she protested in 2010 against the sale of municipal land bought for 5 million dollars and resold for... 1.6 million to developers, at the height of the real estate boom.
70% dirty money in election campaigns

On the investigation which will eventually be implemented, she says she "is following a thread in order to find out how the system - infiltrated by ants - works, to put a stop to the gangrene and catch the culprits."
The process, she says, is "painful but positive."
The wound is being cleaned, but Montreal would need its own investigative unit with ongoing monitoring, to avoid the return of these questionable practices.
How to clean house.
Properly.
